objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Complétez : « Je voudrais du pain, mais je n’ai pas ___ argent. »
options: du
des
un
d’
objectives.explanation: After the negative avoir phrase, the indefinite or partitive quantity becomes de, elided before argent.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Quel groupe complète correctement « Nous avons vu ___ arbre près du puits » ?
options: un bel
un beau
une belle
des beaux
objectives.explanation: Beau becomes bel before a masculine singular noun beginning with a vowel sound.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Complétez : « Ma cousine est ___ Canada pour ses études. »
options: en
au
à la
aux
objectives.explanation: The masculine singular country Canada takes au in this locative expression.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Choisissez la forme qui exprime le futur proche : « Les élèves ___ leurs résultats. »
options: recevaient
ont reçu
vont recevoir
reçoivent
objectives.explanation: Aller in the present plus an infinitive expresses the futur proche.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Complétez : « Quand j’étais petit, je ___ souvent chez ma grand-mère. »
options: ai dormi une seule fois
dormirai
dormirais demain
dormais
objectives.explanation: The imperfect dormais expresses the repeated past habit indicated by souvent and the childhood setting.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Complétez : « Elle parle français plus ___ qu’avant. »
options: couramment
courante
courantes
courants
objectives.explanation: The verb parle is modified by the adverb couramment, not an adjective agreeing with elle.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Quel mot interrogatif convient : « ___ coûte ce dictionnaire ? »
options: Pourquoi
Combien
Qui
Où
objectives.explanation: Combien asks about the price or amount.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Complétez : « Voici le village ___ je suis né. »
options: qui
que
où
dont
objectives.explanation: Où introduces a relative clause referring to a location.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Choisissez l’ordre correct des mots à l’impératif affirmatif.
options: Me donnez le cahier.
Donnez me le cahier.
Moi donnez le cahier.
Donnez-moi le cahier.
objectives.explanation: In the affirmative imperative, the stressed pronoun moi follows the verb and is linked by a hyphen.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Complétez : « Je reste à la maison ___ il pleut très fort. »
options: parce qu’
bien qu’
afin qu’
jusqu’à ce qu’
objectives.explanation: Parce que introduces the stated cause and elides before il; the other conjunctions express different relations and require different constructions here.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Dans un train, un voyageur dit « Pardon, cette place est-elle libre ? » Il cherche surtout à savoir
options: si le billet du train est gratuit.
s’il peut s’asseoir à cet endroit.
si le train a déjà déraillé.
si la gare vend des chaises.
objectives.explanation: Libre describes an unoccupied seat in this context, not free transport.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Quel énoncé annonce une interdiction de stationner ?
options: Vous pouvez vous arrêter ici sans limite.
Le stationnement est conseillé à tous.
Il est interdit de garer un véhicule ici.
Les véhicules doivent être vendus ici.
objectives.explanation: Interdit expresses prohibition; the other choices express permission, advice or an unrelated obligation.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Votre ami vous remercie pour votre aide. Quelle réponse convient ?
options: Je te défends d’entrer.
Il faut acheter un billet.
Je n’ai rien entendu hier.
Je t’en prie.
objectives.explanation: Je t’en prie can politely acknowledge thanks in an informal relationship.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Une affiche porte « Réunion reportée à vendredi ». Que faut-il comprendre ?
options: La réunion aura lieu vendredi au lieu de la date prévue.
La réunion est terminée depuis vendredi dernier.
La réunion aura obligatoirement lieu tous les vendredis.
Personne ne connaît plus le jour de la réunion.
objectives.explanation: Reportée indicates postponement to the stated day, without implying a weekly recurrence.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: « Ce sac appartient à Awa » signifie
options: Awa cherche un sac qui n’est pas à elle.
C’est le sac d’Awa.
Le sac refuse d’entrer chez Awa.
Awa vend tous les sacs de la ville.
objectives.explanation: Appartenir à expresses ownership in this context.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Choisissez la transformation correcte. Réécrivez au pluriel en changeant tous les mots nécessaires : « Cette petite maison est blanche. »
options: Cette petites maisons est blanche.
Ces petit maisons sont blanc.
Ces petites maisons sont blanches.
Ces petites maison est blanches.
objectives.explanation: The demonstrative, noun, adjectives and verb must agree in the plural.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Choisissez la transformation correcte. Mettez à la forme négative avec « ne…jamais » : « Il prend toujours le train. »
options: Il jamais prend ne le train.
Il ne prend toujours jamais le train.
Il prend toujours le train.
Il ne prend jamais le train.
objectives.explanation: Ne surrounds the finite verb with jamais; toujours is replaced.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Choisissez la transformation correcte. Remplacez « les chaussures » par un pronom : « Elle achète les chaussures. »
options: Elle les achète.
Elle leur achète.
Elle y achète.
Elle en achète les chaussures.
objectives.explanation: The feminine plural direct object is replaced by les before the finite verb.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Choisissez la transformation correcte. Transformez à la voix passive en gardant le présent : « Le jardinier arrose les fleurs. »
options: Les fleurs ont arrosé le jardinier.
Les fleurs sont arrosées par le jardinier.
Les fleurs sont arrosé par le jardinier.
Les fleurs seront arrosées par le jardinier.
objectives.explanation: The original object becomes the subject; être stays present and the participle agrees.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Choisissez la transformation correcte. Réunissez avec « dont » sans changer le sens : « Voici le livre. Je t’ai parlé de ce livre. »
options: Voici le livre dont je t’ai parlé de ce livre.
Voici le livre que je t’ai parlé.
Voici le livre dont je t’ai parlé.
Voici le livre où je t’ai parlé.
objectives.explanation: Parler de introduces a de complement, replaced by dont in the relative clause.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Choisissez la transformation correcte. Exprimez une comparaison d’égalité avec « aussi…que » : « Le sac rouge pèse cinq kilos. Le sac bleu pèse cinq kilos. »
options: Le sac rouge est plus lourd que le sac bleu.
Le sac rouge est moins lourd que le sac bleu.
Le sac rouge est aussi lourd le sac bleu.
Le sac rouge est aussi lourd que le sac bleu.
objectives.explanation: The equal weights support equality; either colour may be placed first.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Elle parle d’elle-même : « Je suis prête. » Choisissez le discours indirect au présent après « Elle dit que ».
options: Elle dit qu’elle est prête.
Elle dit que je suis prête.
Elle dit qu’elle était prête.
Elle dit qu’elle sera prête.
objectives.explanation: With the reporting verb in the present, the tense remains present; the speaker becomes elle.

objectives.subject: French
objectives.prompt: Choisissez la transformation correcte. Réécrivez en remplaçant « à la bibliothèque » par « y » : « Nous allons à la bibliothèque après le cours. »
options: Nous allons y après le cours.
Nous y allons après le cours.
Nous y allons à la bibliothèque après le cours.
Nous en allons après le cours.
objectives.explanation: Y replaces the place complement and precedes the finite verb.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: In Genesis 41, what links Joseph’s interpretation of Pharaoh’s dreams to his administrative proposal?
options: He recommends storing grain during plentiful years before the predicted famine.
He recommends distributing all grain in the plentiful years without keeping a reserve.
He recommends importing grain only after the famine has exhausted local supplies.
He recommends leaving storage entirely to Pharaoh’s dream interpreters without administrators.
objectives.explanation: The predicted sequence of abundance and famine leads Joseph to propose advance storage and supervision.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: In Genesis 45, Joseph invites his brothers to come closer during the disclosure of his identity. What best explains the significance of this scene?
options: Joseph keeps his identity secret and questions them only through an interpreter.
He is disclosing his identity and addressing brothers distressed by his presence.
Joseph accuses Benjamin of stealing before ordering the brothers to fetch him.
Joseph negotiates a price for selling the brothers to another official.
objectives.explanation: Joseph identifies himself, asks about his father and reassures his alarmed brothers; the scene is one of recognition and reconciliation.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: Moses’ objection that he is not an effective speaker is answered in Exodus 4 partly by
options: The appointment of Joshua as his spokesman before Pharaoh.
The appointment of Jethro to deliver the message in his place.
the appointment of Aaron to speak with him.
The appointment of Caleb to speak while Moses remains in Midian.
objectives.explanation: Aaron is to serve as spokesman, while Moses receives and communicates the message.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: In Numbers 27, why does Moses request the appointment of a successor?
options: So authority will pass automatically to the oldest of his sons.
So the congregation can remain in the wilderness without anyone leading it.
So the priesthood can be transferred permanently to Pharaoh’s family.
So the community will not be left without leadership.
objectives.explanation: Moses asks for someone to lead the congregation, using the image of sheep without a shepherd.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: Deborah’s role in Judges 4 most directly challenges which assumption?
options: That women are absent from every leadership role in the biblical narrative.
That Barak participates in the campaign.
That a recognised judge can hear disputes brought by Israelites.
That the narrative includes conflict with an opposing army.
objectives.explanation: Deborah is identified as a prophetess and judge who summons and instructs Barak.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: In 1 Samuel 15, Samuel rejects Saul’s attempt to justify retaining livestock for sacrifice because
options: Samuel teaches that livestock can never be offered in any worship.
ritual offerings do not excuse disobedience to the command given.
Saul had been instructed to make himself king of Egypt.
The dispute concerns only the market price of sheep.
objectives.explanation: Samuel’s response contrasts obedience with an attempted sacrificial justification for disobedience.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: What makes Rehoboam’s reply in 1 Kings 12 a failure of responsive leadership?
options: He reduces the burden immediately in response to the elders’ counsel.
He delays his reply until the northern tribes have already accepted his policy.
He promises a heavier burden after the people request relief.
He replaces the requested relief with a plan agreed unanimously by elders and people.
objectives.explanation: Rehoboam follows harsh advice and threatens increased burdens, contributing to division.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: In the Naboth narrative, why is the use of false witnesses especially serious?
options: Naboth had volunteered to sell the vineyard at the offered price.
The witnesses are merely discussing the vineyard’s soil quality.
The dispute ends with Naboth choosing a different vineyard freely.
Legal and religious procedures are manipulated to seize another person’s inheritance.
objectives.explanation: False accusations lead to Naboth’s death and enable Ahab’s seizure of his vineyard.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: Gehazi’s conduct after Naaman’s healing is condemned because he
options: uses deception to obtain gifts that Elisha had refused.
He accepts a gift openly after Elisha authorises him to do so.
He refuses payment but asks Naaman to return to the Jordan.
He reports truthfully that Naaman insisted on thanking Elisha personally.
objectives.explanation: Gehazi falsely attributes a request to Elisha and then lies about his own actions.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: Amos 5 criticises religious celebrations when they coexist with
options: honest judging and concern for the poor.
the denial of justice and oppression of the vulnerable.
fair treatment in public dealings.
repentance expressed through changed conduct.
objectives.explanation: The passage rejects worship detached from justice rather than condemning justice as a substitute for wrongdoing.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: Hosea 6:6 gives priority to which contrast?
options: Military expansion over covenant faithfulness.
Expensive ceremonies over mercy.
Steadfast love and knowledge of God over sacrifice alone.
Royal power over the knowledge of God.
objectives.explanation: Hosea criticises ritual unaccompanied by faithful relationship and steadfast love.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: At Jesus’ baptism in Matthew 3, the heavenly declaration chiefly identifies
options: John’s replacement of Jesus as the promised Son.
The appointment of Jesus to the Jerusalem high priesthood.
The removal of every future test from Jesus’ ministry.
Jesus’ relationship to God and divine approval.
objectives.explanation: The voice identifies Jesus as God’s beloved Son and expresses approval; the narrative does not say temptation has ended.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: In Matthew 4, Jesus’ refusal to jump from the temple demonstrates that
options: scriptural language should not be used to justify testing God.
any quotation of scripture makes an action right.
faith requires deliberately creating danger to demand rescue.
the tempter had offered no scriptural argument.
objectives.explanation: The temptation uses scripture, but Jesus answers with the prohibition against putting God to the test.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: In the call of the fishermen in Mark 1, which response is emphasised?
options: Remaining at work until Jesus guarantees financial security.
Leaving their previous work to follow Jesus.
Requesting formal posts before agreeing to follow him.
Following John while postponing a response to Jesus.
objectives.explanation: The account stresses their prompt response to Jesus’ call rather than a negotiation for status.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: The servant forgiven a large debt in Matthew 18 is later condemned mainly because he
options: cannot calculate the original debt accurately.
forgives his fellow servant before asking the king.
refuses to extend mercy after receiving mercy himself.
asks another servant to keep proper records.
objectives.explanation: The parable highlights the inconsistency between receiving forgiveness and acting mercilessly towards another debtor.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: In Gethsemane, Jesus’ prayer in Matthew 26 holds together
options: complete indifference to suffering and a desire for public office.
a denial that any suffering is possible and a call for revenge.
a command that the disciples arrest the chief priests.
distress and submission to the Father’s will.
objectives.explanation: Jesus expresses anguish while yielding his request to the Father’s will.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: After Peter’s denials in Luke 22, what event immediately leads him to remember Jesus’ warning?
options: The Lord turns and looks at him after the cock crows.
The tearing of the temple curtain as Peter watches.
The darkness at the crucifixion before Peter is questioned.
The return of Judas to the chief priests during Peter’s trial.
objectives.explanation: The look and cockcrow recall the earlier warning, and Peter goes out and weeps.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: What practical problem leads to the selection of the Seven in Acts 6?
options: A dispute about replacing Judas among the Twelve.
Some widows are being overlooked in the daily distribution.
A request that the apostles cease preaching to Gentiles.
A shortage of candidates who had witnessed Jesus’ baptism.
objectives.explanation: The complaint concerns unequal treatment in support distribution; the community appoints suitable people to address it.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: According to Peter in Acts 5, what makes Ananias’s action blameworthy?
options: He refuses a rule that every member must sell land.
He truthfully states he has kept part of the sale money.
He lies about the proceeds rather than being required to surrender property compulsorily.
He asks the apostles whether property may remain unsold.
objectives.explanation: Peter states that the property and proceeds were under Ananias’s control; deception is the issue.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: Acts 2 presents the crowd’s amazement at Pentecost as connected with
options: All listeners abandoning their native languages to learn Aramaic first.
Only Jerusalem residents being permitted to listen.
The crowd understanding solely through a written translation supplied later.
hearing the speakers in the listeners’ own languages.
objectives.explanation: The passage names visitors from many places and describes their surprise at hearing familiar languages.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: Peter’s defence in Acts 11 appeals to the Spirit’s coming upon Gentiles to explain why
options: he should not obstruct God’s acceptance of them.
Gentile acceptance depended first on obtaining Roman citizenship.
The Spirit’s gift should be withheld until every critic approved the visit.
The event had no bearing on questions of fellowship with Gentiles.
objectives.explanation: Peter recounts the events as evidence that the Gentiles received the same divine gift.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: A person offers kind words to a hungry believer but refuses available food. Which teaching in James 2 most directly challenges this?
options: The poor should always be excluded from assemblies.
A claim of faith without practical help is inadequate.
Only public speaking can express faith.
Material needs are irrelevant to the example James gives.
objectives.explanation: James uses unmet needs for clothing and food to show the emptiness of words without action.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: A church reserves good seats for wealthy visitors and tells poor visitors to stand. James 2 identifies this as
options: a necessary test of a visitor’s doctrinal knowledge.
the example of impartial treatment it recommends.
partiality inconsistent with the community’s faith.
proof that wealth determines moral worth.
objectives.explanation: James condemns preferential treatment based on outward wealth.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: James 1 links careful listening with restraint in speaking and anger because
options: anger always proves that a person has listened accurately.
speaking first makes evidence unnecessary.
any disagreement cancels the duty to listen.
human anger does not produce the righteousness God desires.
objectives.explanation: The passage connects readiness to listen with restrained speech and anger.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: Which leadership practice fits 1 Peter 5:2–3?
options: Leading willingly by example rather than dominating those entrusted to one’s care.
Using office principally for dishonest gain.
Treating responsibility as permission to humiliate members.
Avoiding all personal example while demanding compliance.
objectives.explanation: The exhortation contrasts willing, exemplary oversight with exploitation and domination.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: In Genesis 1, the description of humanity’s responsibility towards other living things most directly introduces a theme of
options: humanity’s complete independence from the Creator.
stewardship within creation.
the absence of any responsibility towards other creatures.
creation’s dependence on human beings for its initial existence.
objectives.explanation: The narrative gives humanity a place and responsibility in the created order.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: What does Moses’ intercession after the golden calf episode in Exodus 32 reveal?
options: He denies that the people have broken any command.
He asks that Aaron’s calf become the permanent object of worship.
He pleads for the people despite their wrongdoing.
He offers himself as the ruler who should be worshipped instead.
objectives.explanation: Moses appeals to God’s purposes and promises rather than denying the offence.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: In Joshua 1:7–9, courage is linked especially with
options: rejecting every previous instruction as a sign of strength.
avoiding responsibility until no difficulty remains.
measuring success only by possession of military equipment.
faithfulness to the instruction given, not mere self-confidence.
objectives.explanation: The charge joins courage with attention to the law and assurance of God’s presence.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: In 1 Samuel 3, what does Eli eventually help Samuel recognise?
options: That the repeated call is from the Lord.
That the repeated call is an instruction from Saul.
That Samuel should bring the ark to the battlefield immediately.
That the voice is one of Eli’s sons asking for a sacrifice.
objectives.explanation: Eli instructs Samuel how to respond once he recognises the source of the call.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: David refuses to kill Saul in the camp in 1 Samuel 26 because he
options: He believes Abishai has already killed Saul.
will not strike the Lord’s anointed to obtain the kingdom.
He considers the spear worthless as evidence of access to Saul.
He accepts Abner’s offer to surrender Saul’s army.
objectives.explanation: David takes Saul’s spear and water vessel but rejects killing him as the means of advancement.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: In Solomon’s judgement between the two women, what reveals the true mother’s concern?
options: Her insistence that the child be divided.
Her claim to own a larger house.
Her willingness to surrender her claim so the child may live.
Her ability to pay the king a higher fee.
objectives.explanation: Her compassion for the living child exposes a concern deeper than winning the dispute.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: Elijah’s question about wavering between the Lord and Baal calls the people to
options: combine every rival claim without distinction.
appoint Elijah as an Egyptian governor.
abandon all questions of religious allegiance.
a clear decision about whom they will serve.
objectives.explanation: The challenge at Carmel confronts divided allegiance.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: Josiah’s response to the discovered book of the law begins with
options: distress and a request to inquire of the Lord.
celebration that the people have already fulfilled every command.
a decision that temple repairs remove the need to heed the law.
a refusal to hear the content because the book was found during repairs.
objectives.explanation: Josiah reacts seriously to the gap between the law and the nation’s conduct.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: Why does Nehemiah inspect Jerusalem’s damaged walls before presenting his rebuilding plan?
options: He is attempting to sell the city secretly.
He gathers first-hand knowledge of the condition needing action.
He has already completed all repairs alone.
He intends to prevent anyone from learning that the walls are damaged.
objectives.explanation: His inspection precedes the public call to rebuild and informs the task ahead.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: Daniel 3 presents the three men’s refusal to worship the image as
options: obedience only after receiving a promise of personal advancement.
agreement to worship the image while preserving belief privately.
faithfulness that is not made conditional on guaranteed rescue.
confidence that the image and the Lord have equal authority.
objectives.explanation: They affirm that they will not serve the image even if rescue does not occur.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: Matthew 6:14–15 connects receiving forgiveness with
options: a right to revenge after prayer.
the amount of money given publicly.
membership in a particular occupation.
the duty to forgive others.
objectives.explanation: The teaching refuses to separate prayer for forgiveness from one’s treatment of others.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: Why does Jesus’ call to Matthew provoke a question about association with tax collectors and sinners?
options: His shared meal challenges the critics’ expectations about appropriate company.
He offers Matthew a formal position in the Jerusalem priesthood.
He declares that only people regarded as righteous may share the meal.
He withdraws from the meal to accept the critics’ standard.
objectives.explanation: Jesus’ reply explains his mission using the contrast between the sick needing a physician and those who regard themselves as well.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: In Luke 14:28–33, the examples of a builder and a king principally teach disciples to
options: assume that commitment has no cost.
consider the demands of commitment.
avoid planning because calculation is always faithless.
replace discipleship with the pursuit of military power.
objectives.explanation: The examples concern assessing what an undertaking requires before claiming readiness.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: What narrative role does Joseph of Arimathea perform in Mark 15?
options: He prepares the room for the last meal with the disciples.
He carries Jesus’ cross on the way to execution.
He requests Jesus’ body and arranges its burial.
He supplies the spices brought by the women after the Sabbath.
objectives.explanation: Joseph approaches Pilate, obtains the body and places it in a tomb.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: In Luke 24:13–35, what first occupies the two travellers’ conversation on the road?
options: Jesus’ baptism and John’s imprisonment as events occurring that morning.
The appointment of the Seven and the complaint about the widows.
Peter’s visit to Cornelius and the defence he gives in Jerusalem.
The events surrounding Jesus’ death and reports concerning the empty tomb.
objectives.explanation: The Emmaus account begins with discussion of recent events and disappointed hopes.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: Why do the apostles pray before the selection of Matthias in Acts 1?
options: They seek guidance about which qualified candidate should fill the vacant place.
They seek the selection of a successor to the high priest.
They seek a candidate who has never heard Jesus’ teaching.
They seek permission to end the apostolic witness altogether.
objectives.explanation: The prayer accompanies selection from candidates meeting the stated witness requirement.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: In Acts 4:32–35, the description of shared resources is linked to
options: collecting a private fortune for one apostle.
meeting needs within the believing community.
banning all discussion of material hardship.
ranking members solely by land ownership.
objectives.explanation: The account relates generosity and distribution to the removal of unmet need.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: James 1 compares a hearer who does not act to someone who
options: plants seed and immediately harvests a full crop.
builds an ark before a flood.
looks in a mirror and then forgets what was seen.
gives a feast for a returning son.
objectives.explanation: The mirror image illustrates the failure to turn hearing into sustained action.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: In James 5:16–18, Elijah’s example is used to encourage
options: a decision that prayer belongs only to people unlike ordinary believers.
the conclusion that prayer can never affect a community’s life.
the claim that confession and intercession have no place among believers.
confidence in earnest prayer rather than the belief that only superhuman people can pray.
objectives.explanation: James explicitly presents Elijah as human while describing the effectiveness of his prayer.

objectives.subject: Christian Religious Knowledge (CRK)
objectives.prompt: What purpose does good conduct among non-believers serve in 1 Peter 2:11–12?
options: It provides observable deeds that can challenge hostile accusations.
It guarantees that no one will ever make an accusation.
It permits revenge whenever a believer is criticised.
It requires hiding all ordinary work from neighbours.
objectives.explanation: The passage emphasises conduct visible to others without promising the absence of hostility.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Which statement best expresses tawhid in Islamic teaching?
options: Different gods govern separate parts of creation independently.
A ruler shares Allah’s divine status by holding office.
Worship is directed to Allah alone without partners.
An ancestor becomes divine through the number of descendants.
objectives.explanation: Tawhid affirms divine unity and excludes assigning partners to Allah.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: In Surah al-Fatihah, the request for guidance follows praise and acknowledgement of dependence on Allah. What does this combination emphasise?
options: Guidance is unnecessary once praise has been offered.
Only material wealth is requested in the surah.
The worshipper claims complete independence from Allah.
Worship includes reliance on divine guidance.
objectives.explanation: The surah brings praise, worship, seeking help and the request for guidance together.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Which classroom initiative best applies the emphasis on learning in Qur’an 96:1–5?
options: Helping learners read and understand while recognising the responsibility attached to knowledge.
Treating literacy as unnecessary because knowledge is never acquired.
Restricting books to a few pupils on the basis of family status.
Measuring knowledge only by public praise rather than understanding.
objectives.explanation: The passage associates reading and teaching with the Creator; the scenario applies that emphasis without reducing the verses to a school policy.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: A volunteer humiliates an orphan while claiming to honour Surah ad-Duha. Which aspect of the surah most directly contradicts this behaviour?
options: Its instruction to restrict all learning to adults.
Its instruction against harsh treatment of the orphan.
Its command that every gift be exchanged for money.
Its rule that only travellers deserve respectful speech.
objectives.explanation: The closing moral instructions include care in dealing with an orphan and a person asking for help.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Surah al-Kafirun rejects a proposed sharing of worship. Which conclusion best stays within that teaching?
options: Every disagreement requires personal abuse.
Distinct beliefs mean neighbours can never cooperate in ordinary matters.
Commitment to worship is not exchanged for a compromise of belief.
The surah instructs believers to worship every deity in turn.
objectives.explanation: The surah affirms distinct religious commitment; it does not prescribe insulting neighbours or alternating worship.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Surah an-Nas directs the seeker of refuge to Allah against
options: all forms of advice offered by other people.
only physical illness, without reference to inward influence.
the act of seeking guidance through prayer.
harmful whispering that can come through jinn or human beings.
objectives.explanation: The surah identifies the source of refuge and the danger of whispering, including human and jinn sources.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: A trader uses a balance that shows more than the actual weight supplied. Which principle in Qur’an 17:35 is violated?
options: Giving accurate measure and using a just balance.
Providing goods in response to a customer’s order.
Recording the date of a sale.
Explaining the price before payment.
objectives.explanation: The verse requires fair measurement; a deliberately misleading balance defeats that requirement.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: A student publicly promises to return borrowed equipment but deliberately keeps it. Qur’an 61:2–3 most directly challenges
options: the use of equipment in a classroom.
the contradiction between professed words and deliberate conduct.
the practice of borrowing with permission.
the keeping of a written lending record.
objectives.explanation: The passage condemns declaring what one does not do.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: According to Qur’an 17:23–24, caring for ageing parents should include
options: mocking them when assistance takes time.
responding with contempt if they repeat a request.
respectful speech and compassionate treatment.
treating prayer for them as a reason to withhold all kindness.
objectives.explanation: The verses connect kindness, restrained speech, humility and prayer for parents.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Qur’an 31:15 describes parents urging a child towards shirk. What balance does it teach?
options: Obey the demand because every parental instruction overrides faith.
Abandon all respectful conduct towards them.
Accept shirk privately while denying it publicly.
Do not obey that demand, but continue treating them kindly in worldly life.
objectives.explanation: The verse distinguishes refusal of a wrongful religious demand from the continuing duty of good companionship.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: In Hadith terminology, what is the isnad?
options: The chain of people transmitting a report.
The textual content of the transmitted report.
The legal judgement drawn from applying a report.
The designation of a report as weak or sound.
objectives.explanation: The isnad identifies a report’s transmission chain; the matn is its textual content.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: A teacher separates the wording attributed to the Prophet from the names through whom it was reported. The wording is called the
options: isnad.
matn.
rawi.
sahih.
objectives.explanation: Matn refers to the text of a report, distinguished from its chain of transmission.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Two people perform the same outward charitable act for different purposes. An-Nawawi Hadith 1 draws attention especially to
options: the public similarity of the two actions alone.
only the number of spectators for each action.
their intentions.
the assumption that an outward deed reveals its entire purpose.
objectives.explanation: The teaching makes motive central to the moral evaluation of action; appearance alone does not disclose it.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: A learner wants useful revision materials for himself but hides the only shared copy from classmates. Which teaching of an-Nawawi Hadith 13 is most relevant?
options: Treating shared resources as private property once touched.
Assuming personal success requires every classmate’s failure.
Restricting all kindness to people who provide a reward.
Wishing comparable good for another as for oneself.
objectives.explanation: The hadith challenges self-centred standards of goodwill; the revision scenario is an original application.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: An unverified accusation arrives in a class discussion group. Which response best applies the speech principle in an-Nawawi Hadith 15?
options: Avoid spreading harmful claims and use speech responsibly.
Forward it privately because private sharing cannot cause harm.
Repeat it with a disclaimer while making no effort to check it.
Treat participation in every conversation as a duty regardless of content.
objectives.explanation: The hadith links faith with beneficial speech or restraint; forwarding a damaging unverified claim does not fulfil that principle.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: After an insult, a player pauses instead of striking another player. This most directly applies an-Nawawi Hadith 16 through
options: denial that any disagreement occurred.
restraint of anger in conduct.
a claim that unfairness must never be reported.
a decision to punish everyone at the event.
objectives.explanation: The counsel against anger calls for self-control, not a requirement to conceal or endorse wrongdoing.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: In an-Nawawi Hadith 18, good conduct is required
options: only when an audience can verify the person’s reputation.
only after a harmful deed has brought a visible penalty.
beyond situations where other people are watching.
only in formal acts of worship rather than ordinary relationships.
objectives.explanation: The hadith joins consciousness of Allah wherever one is with good deeds and good character towards people.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Which distinction between zakat and voluntary sadaqah is most accurate?
options: Zakat means any personal purchase; sadaqah means compulsory tax in every case.
Both terms always mean a payment only during Hajj.
Voluntary sadaqah cancels every zakat obligation automatically.
Zakat is a prescribed obligation under its conditions; voluntary sadaqah is additional giving.
objectives.explanation: The distinction concerns the prescribed obligation and additional voluntary charity, not an automatic substitution of one for the other.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Qur’an 2:183 associates fasting particularly with developing
options: taqwa, or consciousness of Allah.
a guarantee that abstention excuses dishonest speech.
the view that hunger itself cancels all other responsibilities.
public prestige as the sole measure of a fast’s value.
objectives.explanation: The verse gives a moral and spiritual aim rather than merely describing abstention from food.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: In Qur’an 3:97, the obligation of pilgrimage is stated with reference to
options: only those already living in Makkah.
those able to undertake the journey.
only those who have completed Umrah first in a different year.
every individual without regard to capacity.
objectives.explanation: Ability is expressly relevant to the obligation; practical assessment of a person’s circumstances requires appropriate guidance.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Tayammum differs from ordinary wudu principally because it involves
options: a purification made solely by washing with a larger amount of water.
a separate form of charity offered instead of ritual purity.
ritual purification using clean earth when its conditions apply.
a pilgrimage rite that replaces the need for purification.
objectives.explanation: Tayammum is an alternative mode of ritual purification under specified circumstances, not a replacement for worship as a whole.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: In early Islamic history, the Hijrah to Madinah refers to
options: the first revelation at Hira.
the Farewell Pilgrimage from Madinah to Makkah.
the journey known as al-Isra and al-Mi‘raj.
the migration from Makkah to Madinah.
objectives.explanation: The Hijrah is the migration that marks a major stage in the community’s development; it is distinct from revelation and other journeys.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Which sequence correctly orders the first four caliphs in the standard Sunni historical account?
options: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali.
Umar, Abu Bakr, Ali, Uthman.
Uthman, Ali, Abu Bakr, Umar.
Ali, Uthman, Umar, Abu Bakr.
objectives.explanation: The conventional sequence is Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali; naming the account avoids implying identical evaluations across all traditions.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: The production of standard copies of the Qur’an under Caliph Uthman chiefly addressed a concern about
options: replacing the Arabic revelation with a new biography.
disputes and differences arising in recitation among expanding communities.
ending the use of written copies in favour of memory alone.
postponing every recitation until a new revelation arrived.
objectives.explanation: The account in Sahih al-Bukhari describes concern over recitation differences and the preparation and distribution of copies.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Why is publicly honouring a respected teacher different from treating that teacher as divine in Islamic belief?
options: Any expression of gratitude automatically makes a person divine.
Teaching gives a person independent divine power.
Respect for a person does not give that person a share in Allah’s divinity.
A large following removes the distinction between Creator and creature.
objectives.explanation: Tawhid distinguishes ordinary human respect from attributing divinity or worship to a human being.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: What relationship between creation and learning is expressed in Qur’an 96:1–5?
options: Human knowledge is presented as wholly independent of any teaching.
The pen is mentioned only as a device for collecting tax.
Reading is presented as a substitute for acknowledging the Creator.
Allah is presented as Creator and the source of teaching.
objectives.explanation: The passage places the call to read alongside creation and teaching, including teaching by the pen.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Surah ad-Duha reminds its addressee of past divine care. How does the surah connect that reminder to conduct?
options: It follows reassurance with duties towards vulnerable people and acknowledgement of blessing.
It treats past hardship as permission to humiliate others.
It uses reassurance to cancel concern for people seeking help.
It makes gratitude depend on receiving praise from those helped.
objectives.explanation: The closing verses move from remembered care to obligations in speech and treatment of others.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: In Qur’an study, a surah is best described as
options: a verse within a chapter.
a chapter of the Qur’an.
a commentary explaining a Qur’anic passage.
a chain of transmitters attached to a report.
objectives.explanation: A surah is a Qur’anic chapter; the other descriptions concern different areas of study.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Qur’an 17:106 links the gradual revelation of the Qur’an with what manner of presenting it to people?
options: Withholding every part until no audience remained.
Replacing earlier revelation with a private commentary.
Recitation in portions at intervals.
Allowing each listener to compose a new surah.
objectives.explanation: The verse relates revelation in stages to reciting the Qur’an to people at a measured pace; gradual revelation is not the creation of a later text.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Which description best distinguishes shirk from an ordinary mistake in arithmetic?
options: Shirk means any wrong answer on any subject.
Every calculation automatically constitutes worship.
Shirk is another name for the dawn prayer.
Shirk concerns associating partners with Allah, rather than every kind of error.
objectives.explanation: The doctrinal term has a specific meaning and should not be extended to every unrelated error.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: In Qur’an 2:285, belief in the messengers is presented as part of
options: the believer’s confession of faith.
only an additional custom unrelated to belief.
a requirement to reject all messengers before Muhammad.
an entitlement to choose which messengers deserve belief solely by ethnicity.
objectives.explanation: The passage links belief in Allah, angels, books and messengers; it does not treat earlier messengers as objects of hostility.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Which conduct most directly contradicts Qur’an 2:42?
options: Correcting a mistaken statement after checking it.
Knowingly mixing truth with falsehood and hiding what is true.
Admitting that one does not know an answer.
Presenting an accurate record despite personal inconvenience.
objectives.explanation: The verse addresses distortion and concealment of truth.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: A shopkeeper discovers that an assistant’s measuring container is too small. Which action best implements fair dealing?
options: Continue using it while displaying a religious slogan.
Blame customers for not bringing their own containers.
Replace or correct the measure and address customers’ shortfalls honestly.
Keep it for customers unlikely to complain.
objectives.explanation: The requirement of fair measurement calls for correcting the practice, not merely declaring honesty.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Qur’an 5:90–91 identifies which social danger associated with gambling?
options: A guarantee that every participant becomes wealthy.
The removal of every source of conflict.
Automatic fulfilment of obligations towards dependants.
Enmity and hostility among people.
objectives.explanation: The passage associates gambling with conflict and distraction from remembrance and prayer.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: A person cares for parents politely in public but habitually insults them at home. Which criticism follows from Qur’an 17:23–24?
options: Respectful treatment is an ongoing duty, not a public performance only.
Public courtesy makes all private mistreatment acceptable.
Financial provision always cancels the duty of respectful speech.
Only neighbours are entitled to gentle treatment.
objectives.explanation: The verses describe the relationship with parents, including speech and compassion, rather than merely public appearances.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Why is a long chain of names alone insufficient to establish that a Hadith is authentic?
options: Every long chain is automatically fabricated.
Transmission also requires critical assessment of continuity and narrators’ reliability.
The report’s text can never be examined.
A report becomes authentic when names are alphabetised.
objectives.explanation: Hadith criticism evaluates transmission and content through recognised criteria; counting names alone is inadequate.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Which term commonly denotes a weak Hadith in the classification studied at this level?
options: Sahih.
Hasan.
Da‘if.
Matn.
objectives.explanation: Da‘if denotes weakness in classification; matn identifies a report’s text rather than its grade.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Which pair of duties appears alongside responsible speech in an-Nawawi Hadith 15?
options: Completing Hajj and collecting every debt immediately.
Performing trade and refusing hospitality.
Studying genealogy and increasing personal rank.
Generosity towards the neighbour and guest.
objectives.explanation: The hadith connects faith with speech, neighbourly generosity and hospitality.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: An-Nawawi Hadith 34 describes responses to wrongdoing in relation to
options: a person’s ability to act, speak or reject it inwardly.
the speaker’s popularity rather than capacity.
the assumption that inward disapproval is identical to public approval.
the requirement to use the same outward response in every circumstance.
objectives.explanation: The text distinguishes ability and modes of response. It should not be turned into unrestricted permission for coercion.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Which pairing correctly links an Islamic worship term with its basic meaning?
options: Zakat — the evening obligatory prayer.
Sawm — fasting.
Hajj — purification before daily prayer.
Wudu — fasting from dawn until sunset.
objectives.explanation: Sawm refers to fasting; the other pairings confuse distinct terms.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Which of these is expressly named among the recipients of zakat in Qur’an 9:60?
options: Every wealthy person solely because of wealth.
Only relatives of the collector regardless of need or category.
People burdened by debt.
Only owners of shops that supply the collection office.
objectives.explanation: Debtors are among the listed categories; being wealthy, related or a supplier is not by itself a listed entitlement.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: What does Qur’an 2:184–185 provide for a person who is ill or travelling in relation to Ramadan fasting?
options: A command that no missed day can ever be made up.
An instruction that every traveller must abandon fasting permanently.
A rule that illness is never relevant to the obligation.
A concession involving making up days, under the stated conditions.
objectives.explanation: The passage addresses illness and travel and completing the number of days; individual cases may require qualified guidance.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Why should studying the social purposes of zakat include the recipients as well as the giver?
options: The institution concerns support and distribution, not only the giver’s self-description.
Recipients have no role in the institution.
Only the giver’s public praise determines who is eligible.
Any recipient becomes responsible for paying the giver a profit.
objectives.explanation: The stated recipient categories and distributive purpose make the receiving side essential to understanding zakat.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Which distinction between compilation and standardisation of the Qur’an is most defensible?
options: Compilation is the first revelation, while standardisation is every later revelation.
Collecting material and preparing consistent authorised copies are related but different preservation activities.
Compilation and standardisation both mean translating the text into another language.
Compilation excludes written material, while standardisation excludes all recitation.
objectives.explanation: The preservation accounts distinguish collecting written material from later preparation and distribution of standard copies.

objectives.subject: Islamic Religious Knowledge (IRK)
objectives.prompt: Why was migration to Madinah more than a change of geographical residence for the early Muslim community?
options: It removed every later difference or conflict within the community.
It made the earlier Makkan revelation no longer applicable.
It enabled the development of an organised communal life in a new setting.
It restricted communal obligations to those born in Madinah.
objectives.explanation: The Hijrah’s significance includes community formation; it did not automatically remove all later challenges.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: In the original sentence “The news struck her like a stone against a window”, the comparison primarily suggests
options: a carefully measured exchange.
a quiet, gradual reassurance.
a deliberate physical attack on a real window.
a sudden, disturbing impact.
objectives.explanation: The explicit like-comparison transfers the shock of a stone hitting glass to the effect of news.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: A speaker calls the community library “a harbour for restless minds”. The metaphor presents reading as
options: a means of transporting goods by water.
a source of refuge and support for thought.
a guarantee that all uncertainty disappears forever.
an activity possible only beside the sea.
objectives.explanation: Harbour is transferred from a place of shelter for boats to the library’s intellectual and emotional role.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: Which device is most evident in “Dawn tiptoed through the shutters”?
options: Allusion.
A rhetorical question.
Euphemism.
Personification.
objectives.explanation: Dawn is given the human action of moving on tiptoe.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: “I have corrected this sentence a million times,” a tired editor says after several revisions. The exaggeration chiefly conveys
options: frustration with repeated effort.
an exact record of the revision count.
a comparison between two kinds of punctuation.
the editor’s confidence that no changes were needed.
objectives.explanation: The implausibly large number intensifies frustration rather than supplying literal data.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: Which expression contains an oxymoron?
options: A memory that slowly fades.
A memory of a quiet street.
A memory from last year.
A painfully pleasant memory.
objectives.explanation: Painfully and pleasant bring apparently contradictory qualities into one compact expression.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: A chairman says, “Everyone must be heard,” then switches off the microphone whenever anyone disagrees. The irony lies chiefly in
options: the fact that a meeting has a chairman.
the use of a microphone in a public setting.
the absence of an audience at the meeting.
the contradiction between his declared principle and his conduct.
objectives.explanation: The actions undermine the promise of open participation.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: A cracked cup appears when a family separates and again when reconciliation begins. Its recurring use most plausibly makes it
options: a narrator with independent knowledge of events.
a rhyme scheme connecting the two scenes.
a symbol of a damaged relationship that may be repaired.
proof that the story is a technical guide to pottery.
objectives.explanation: The object acquires a significance beyond its practical function through its repeated connection with the relationship.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: Early in a story, the narrator briefly notices a bridge plank lifting under a passing cart. Much later the bridge fails. The early detail functions as
options: an interruption by a new narrator.
a final resolution.
a retrospective summary after the failure.
foreshadowing.
objectives.explanation: The early warning prepares for a later event without narrating it in advance.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: A narrative pauses a present-day reunion to recount the friends’ quarrel ten years earlier. This interruption is
options: a prophecy of an event not yet lived.
a change from prose to dialogue as a genre.
the final resolution of the reunion.
a flashback.
objectives.explanation: The account moves back from its current narrative time to an earlier event.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: A chapter ends just as a character opens a sealed envelope, withholding its contents until the next chapter. This arrangement chiefly creates
options: a reliable summary of every character’s future.
a change from first-person to omniscient narration.
a complete resolution of the main uncertainty.
suspense.
objectives.explanation: Delaying the information encourages anticipation about what the envelope contains.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: Without calling her meticulous, a story shows a trader arranging every receipt by date and checking each entry twice. This is chiefly
options: a narrator’s account of events outside the story.
direct characterisation through an explicit label.
a change in the story’s historical period.
indirect characterisation through behaviour.
objectives.explanation: Readers infer the trait from repeated actions rather than being told the adjective.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: A reckless cousin is placed beside a cautious protagonist so that their choices highlight each other. The cousin functions as a
options: narrator by definition.
setting.
foil.
chorus by definition.
objectives.explanation: A foil’s contrasting qualities bring another character’s traits into sharper focus.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: A fictional official is generous to relatives, harsh towards employees and privately ashamed of his behaviour. These contrasting qualities most directly support describing him as
options: a flat character defined by one unchanging trait.
a setting rather than a participant.
an omniscient narrator solely because he has thoughts.
a round character.
objectives.explanation: Several conflicting dimensions give the character complexity; complexity alone does not prove change over time.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: Over the course of a novel, a timid apprentice learns to challenge unfair decisions. This development chiefly makes the apprentice
options: a static character.
a third-person narrator.
a dynamic character.
a stage direction.
objectives.explanation: Dynamic describes meaningful change during the narrative, not whether a character is physically active.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: A minor character keeps the same outlook despite several events that transform others. Which term concerns this absence of development?
options: Omniscient.
Retrospective.
Round.
Static.
objectives.explanation: Static concerns remaining substantially unchanged; it does not itself determine psychological complexity.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: Which statement about a protagonist is most accurate?
options: The protagonist is necessarily the first character mentioned.
The protagonist occupies the central role even when morally flawed.
The protagonist must always be morally admirable.
The protagonist must be the narrator in every story.
objectives.explanation: Narrative centrality, rather than moral perfection or order of appearance, defines the role.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: A novel’s main character struggles against a discriminatory institution rather than one named villain. Which interpretation is defensible?
options: The antagonistic force can be institutional.
The main character ceases to be a protagonist.
A story cannot contain conflict without one individual villain.
An institution must therefore be the narrator.
objectives.explanation: Opposition to a protagonist’s aims need not come from a single person.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: “I saw Hauwa fold the note, but I could not tell what she intended.” What restriction is explicit in this first-person narration?
options: The narrator observes Hauwa without direct access to her intention.
The narrator has already explained Hauwa’s motive with certainty.
The narrator is absent from the scene.
The narrator knows every character’s private thought.
objectives.explanation: The distinction between seeing an action and knowing its motive establishes limited access.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: In one passage a narrator reveals what two separated characters are privately thinking at the same moment. This most clearly demonstrates
options: a single eyewitness’s ordinary visual observation.
a narrator limited to one character’s spoken words.
the complete absence of narration.
omniscient access.
objectives.explanation: Access to both private minds exceeds a viewpoint confined to one observer.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: Which account most clearly presents a causal plot rather than merely a sequence?
options: The gate was blue, and the wall was white.
The guard arrived, and the visitors arrived afterwards.
The visitors had bags, and the guard had a chair.
The guard lost the key, so the late visitors could not enter.
objectives.explanation: Losing the key explains why entry fails, connecting events through cause and consequence.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: A scene occurs outside a locked polling station after voting has ended. Which detail most directly establishes its temporal setting?
options: The building serves as a polling station.
The station has a locked entrance.
People can stand outside the building.
Voting has already ended.
objectives.explanation: The end of voting locates the scene in time; the other details concern place or physical circumstances.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: A witness wants to protect a friend but also wants to give truthful evidence. The central conflict described is
options: a disagreement between a narrator and an author.
internal conflict between competing loyalties.
a contrast between two geographical settings.
a physical struggle between two armies.
objectives.explanation: The struggle occurs within the witness’s choices and values.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: At the decisive point in a story, a councillor must publicly accept or reject a bribe, and that decision settles the central struggle. This moment is the
options: background setting.
opening catalogue of characters.
exposition.
climax.
objectives.explanation: The decisive confrontation at maximum tension forms the narrative climax.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: After the central dispute is settled, a final chapter shows its consequences for the families. This chapter chiefly provides
options: a preliminary hint of the dispute.
a denouement.
a complication preceding every conflict.
the initial exposition.
objectives.explanation: A denouement resolves or explores the aftermath of the main action.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: The opening pages introduce a household, its location and an old disagreement before the main action begins. Their chief function is
options: exposition.
the concealment of all background information.
the resolution of an already completed conflict.
the final reversal.
objectives.explanation: Exposition supplies background needed to understand later action.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: A comic story shows an “Office for Reducing Forms” demanding twelve forms before accepting a complaint about paperwork. Its chief satirical target is
options: the physical difficulty of reading every alphabet.
bureaucratic inefficiency and self-contradiction.
the beauty of handwriting as a private hobby.
the impossibility of running any public office.
objectives.explanation: The comic contradiction exposes an institution reproducing the problem it claims to solve.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: The audience sees a thief hide behind a curtain. A character then assures everyone that the room is empty. The scene creates dramatic irony because
options: all characters and spectators have identical information.
the audience knows something the speaking character does not.
the speaking character knows more than the audience.
the curtain has become the narrator.
objectives.explanation: Unequal knowledge makes the assurance ironic for the audience.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: Alone on stage, a character speaks thoughts that no other character hears. This convention is a
options: dialogue.
conversation between a chorus and a crowd.
stage direction.
soliloquy.
objectives.explanation: A soliloquy externalises private thought in dramatic speech.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: A character briefly addresses the audience while the other characters are conventionally treated as unable to hear. This is an
options: act division.
ordinary reply addressed to every character present.
expository footnote.
aside.
objectives.explanation: An aside gives selected speech to the audience without making it part of the other characters’ shared hearing.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: In a script, “[The light narrows to a circle around the empty chair]” is primarily
options: the title of a new genre.
an author’s bibliography.
a stage direction shaping visual emphasis.
a spoken declaration by the chair.
objectives.explanation: The bracketed instruction governs performance and focuses attention through lighting.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: What does Sade’s repeated hiding of the letter most strongly suggest?
options: She intends to sell the letter to a customer.
She is uncertain how her plans will be received.
She has already discussed every detail with her mother.
She cannot recognise the language of the letter.
objectives.explanation: Her concealment, repeated reading and prepared argument indicate apprehension about a response.
objectives.passage: Sade placed the letter beneath a length of blue cloth whenever a customer entered. By noon she had read the first line so often that the paper had softened at the fold. Her mother worked the sewing machine without asking about it. Last month, when Sade mentioned the design scholarship, her mother had counted the unfinished uniforms and said nothing. Now the machine stopped. Sade prepared her argument about earning money while studying, but her mother reached into a biscuit tin and brought out a tape measure. Its numbers had faded where years of fingers had held it. “You will need one of your own,” she said. Sade unfolded the letter. For the first time that morning, she read beyond the word “Congratulations”. Outside, someone called for a uniform; neither woman answered immediately.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: The mother’s gift of a tape measure chiefly communicates
options: practical support for Sade’s future training.
proof that the scholarship has been cancelled.
an instruction to complete all uniforms before reading.
a demand that Sade abandon design entirely.
objectives.explanation: The words about needing her own measure turn the gift into encouragement for a next stage.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: Why is the detail of the faded numbers on the tape measure significant?
options: It connects the mother’s long working experience with the daughter’s opportunity.
It establishes that the letter is several decades old.
It proves that the scholarship requires an examination in arithmetic.
It shows that neither woman has ever used sewing tools.
objectives.explanation: The wear records years of labour, giving emotional weight to the transfer of the tool.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: Which account of the narrative viewpoint is most accurate?
options: The mother narrates the scene directly in the first person.
The third-person narration gives access to Sade’s anticipation while presenting her mother largely through actions.
An unnamed customer describes both women’s private thoughts equally.
The passage consists entirely of dialogue without narration.
objectives.explanation: Sade’s prepared argument is disclosed; the mother’s response emerges through silence, stopping work and giving the measure.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: The final unanswered call for a uniform mainly serves to
options: pause the ordinary work routine around an important private moment.
show that the customer has never visited before.
prove that both women have permanently stopped sewing.
announce a violent dispute in the street.
objectives.explanation: The momentary delay contrasts the continuing demands of work with the significance of the exchange.

For the first time that morning, she read beyond the word “Congratulations”. Outside, someone called for a uniform; neither woman answered immediately.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: The contrast between imagined applause and actual silence chiefly reveals
options: the audience’s deliberate plan to destroy the drum.
the narrator’s dislike of every form of music.
the uncle’s refusal to let the narrator perform.
the difference between anticipated success and the anxiety of beginning.
objectives.explanation: The narrator imagined recognition but had not prepared emotionally for the exposed moment before playing.
objectives.passage: I arrived at the square carrying the drum my uncle had lent me. All week I had imagined the applause after my first solo. I had not imagined the silence before it. The other drummers waited beneath the neem tree, their hands resting on their instruments. Someone shifted a bench. Someone coughed. I tightened a rope that needed no tightening. When my uncle nodded, I struck the opening pattern too quickly. The older players did not correct me aloud; they slowed their own beat until I could find it. Only then did the faces in front of us separate into people I knew. Afterwards, my uncle asked whether I had enjoyed playing alone. I began to say yes, then looked at the men packing their drums beside mine. “Not quite alone,” I said.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: What does tightening a rope that needs no tightening imply about the narrator?
options: The performance has already ended successfully.
The narrator is correcting the older drummers’ instruments.
The borrowed drum has certainly broken beyond repair.
Nervousness is finding expression in an unnecessary action.
objectives.explanation: The explicit absence of need makes the action a sign of unease rather than routine repair.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: How do the older players respond to the hurried opening?
options: They adjust their playing to help the narrator recover the rhythm.
They stop the performance and rebuke the narrator publicly.
They leave the square without playing.
They increase their speed until the narrator gives up.
objectives.explanation: Slowing their own beat provides support without a spoken correction.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: In the final reply, “Not quite alone” revises the narrator’s earlier understanding of a solo by recognising
options: that no part of the performance was played by the narrator.
that the uncle had secretly replaced the drum.
that the audience heard nothing throughout the event.
the support of other performers within an individual achievement.
objectives.explanation: The glance at the other drummers connects the apparent solo success with their assistance.
objectives.passage: I arrived at the square carrying the drum my uncle had lent me. All week I had imagined the applause after my first solo. I had not imagined the silence before it. The other drummers waited beneath the neem tree, their hands resting on their instruments. Someone shifted a bench. Someone coughed. I tightened a rope that needed no tightening. When my uncle nodded, I struck the opening pattern too quickly. The older players did not correct me aloud; they slowed their own beat until I could find it. Only then did the faces in front of us separate into people I knew. Afterwards, my uncle asked whether I had enjoyed playing alone. I began to say yes, then looked at the men packing their drums beside mine. “Not quite alone,” I said.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: Which description best captures the movement of the narrator’s attitude?
options: From enthusiasm for music to permanent rejection of performance.
From confidence in the uncle to certainty that he is an enemy.
From complete indifference to a desire to compete in sport.
From imagining personal applause to recognising shared contribution.
objectives.explanation: The opening centres anticipated praise; the ending acknowledges the people who sustained the performance.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: In “the washing line writes white”, the image chiefly transforms the drying clothes into
options: a description of rain dissolving ink.
marks made across the space of the yard.
evidence that the yard has been painted permanently.
a literal letter written by a bus driver.
objectives.explanation: Writes turns the visual arrangement of pale washing into an act of inscription.
objectives.passage:
At dawn the washing line writes white across the yard.
Shirts lift their empty arms towards the road;
I pin my father’s coat beside my school dress,
and watch the sleeves grow restless in the wind.
Beyond our wall, the buses gather speed.
My dress leans outward, held by two small pegs.

objectives.prompt: The shirts’ “empty arms” give the clothes a suggestion of
options: an exact count of the people travelling on the buses.
human movement despite the absence of bodies inside them.
a conversation spoken by the father.
complete physical stillness throughout the poem.
objectives.explanation: Arms and lifting animate the garments while empty keeps their bodily absence in view.

Summer rainfall and winter snowfall.
Silence outdoors and a loud conversation indoors.
Free movement along the road and movement constrained by attachment.
objectives.explanation: The buses gather speed while the leaning dress remains held by pegs.

options: the material privilege surrounding the chairman’s public words.

before they opened up the hall.
Its velvet waited, red and still,

At dusk they carried out the chair;
the neighbours slowly left the wall.

objectives.explanation: A biography concerns another person’s life; an autobiography is written by its subject.

objectives.explanation: A memoir can focus on a selected period or theme of the writer’s lived experience.

objectives.passage: Everyone called me the fearless watchman. I did not discourage them. When the shopkeepers asked about the shape I had seen near the warehouse, I described a figure tall enough to reach the roof. In truth, I had seen only its shadow, stretched by the security lamp. I left that detail out. My account grew with each retelling until even I could picture the stranger’s face. Then little Emeka arrived carrying a broken umbrella. He opened it beneath the lamp, and the wall filled with the same enormous shoulders. The shopkeepers laughed. I laughed too, loudly enough, I hoped, to sound like a man who had understood the joke from the beginning. That evening I moved my chair closer to the light, though I told everyone the new position was cooler.

objectives.explanation: The repeated shape on the wall links the earlier impression to an umbrella shadow.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: Which loss matters most to Binta as the passage presents it?
options: The familiar social rhythm attached to the cinema.
A newly purchased wardrobe that has gone missing.
The refusal of the new owner to speak to her.
The destruction of the mango tree.
objectives.explanation: The absent queue and familiar paired arrivals show the loss of a shared routine, beyond a change in building use.
objectives.passage: The old cinema became a furniture store in August. Binta, who had sold groundnuts by its doorway for twenty years, watched the painted stars disappear beneath a coat of cream. On the first Saturday, she set out her tray at the usual hour. No queue formed. A delivery driver asked whether she could move so that his men could carry in a wardrobe. She shifted to the shade of a mango tree. From there she could still see the doorway, but it no longer framed the familiar faces arriving in pairs. At sunset the new owner brought out a chair. “You might be more comfortable,” he said. Binta thanked him and sat. For years she had wanted a place to rest during the interval. Now the interval seemed to have swallowed the entire evening.

objectives.explanation: The owner is considerate, so the change cannot be reduced to a simple contrast between one villain and a victim.

objectives.subject: Literature in English
objectives.prompt: Which stage action gives the audience information not yet openly acknowledged in the dialogue?
options: The clerk substitutes a fresh ledger page before the auditor enters.

objectives.explanation: The opening direction shows a substitution that the clerk’s claim of perfect agreement does not disclose.
objectives.passage:
[A council records room. A sealed envelope lies on the desk. Behind the desk, the CLERK replaces a page in a ledger with a freshly written sheet. The AUDITOR enters before the CLERK can put away the original.]
AUDITOR: I have come for the record, not your summary of it.
CLERK: They agree perfectly.
[The CLERK slides the original page beneath the envelope.]
AUDITOR: Then comparison will take very little time.
CLERK: The chairman expects us in five minutes.
AUDITOR: We should not keep him waiting for an inaccurate account.
[The AUDITOR pulls a chair towards the desk. The CLERK remains standing, one hand resting on the envelope.]
