Explain a distinct constraint such as substitution, postponement or applicable regulation. (3 marks)

theory.question: A household holds ₦50,000 in cash while the relevant price index rises from 100 to 125. Express the later cash balance in base-period purchasing-power naira and explain the change.
theory.modelAnswer: Real value = 50,000×100/125 = ₦40,000 in base-period purchasing power. The nominal balance remains ₦50,000, but its purchasing power is 20% below the original base-period value.
markingPoints: Use cash × base index/current index. (2 marks)
Calculate ₦40,000. (2 marks)
Distinguish unchanged nominal money from the 20% real-value loss. (2 marks)

theory.question: Explain why adding the full value of flour sold to a baker to the full value of the bread sold to households would overstate final output. State one correct way to avoid the error.
theory.modelAnswer: The bread’s value already includes the flour used to produce it, so adding both full values counts the flour twice. Count final bread only, or sum value added at each production stage.
markingPoints: Explain that flour is an intermediate input embodied in bread. (2 marks)
Explain double counting of the same contribution. (2 marks)
Give a valid final-output or value-added method. (2 marks)

theory.question: A council proposes a flat ₦2,000 monthly service levy on every household. Compare the burden on households earning ₦20,000 and ₦100,000 per month, and explain one equity concern.
theory.modelAnswer: The levy is 10% of ₦20,000 and 2% of ₦100,000. It therefore takes a greater share from the lower-income household, which may reduce its ability to pay for essentials. The levy is regressive relative to income in this comparison.
markingPoints: Calculate 10% for the lower-income household. (1 mark)
Calculate 2% for the higher-income household. (1 mark)
Explain the regressive income burden. (2 marks)
Explain a relevant equity concern. (2 marks)

theory.question: Country X can use a fixed resource bundle to produce either 12 tonnes of cocoa or 6 tonnes of rubber. Country Y can produce either 8 tonnes of cocoa or 8 tonnes of rubber. Assuming straight-line frontiers, identify each country’s comparative advantage and justify your answer.
theory.modelAnswer: In X, one tonne of cocoa costs 6/12 = 0.5 tonne of rubber; in Y it costs 8/8 = 1 tonne of rubber, so X has comparative advantage in cocoa. One tonne of rubber costs 2 tonnes of cocoa in X but 1 in Y, so Y has comparative advantage in rubber.
markingPoints: Calculate cocoa opportunity costs in X and Y. (2 marks)
Conclude X has comparative advantage in cocoa. (1 mark)
Calculate rubber opportunity costs in X and Y. (2 marks)
Conclude Y has comparative advantage in rubber. (1 mark)

theory.question: Describe two structural differences between a typical photosynthetic leaf cell and a typical animal cheek cell. Explain one functional consequence.
theory.modelAnswer: The leaf cell has a cellulose wall and chloroplasts; the cheek cell lacks both. The wall supports the plant cell and resists excessive swelling, while chloroplasts allow photosynthesis.
markingPoints: First correct paired structural difference. (2 marks)
Second distinct correct paired structural difference. (2 marks)
Explain a relevant functional consequence. (2 marks)

theory.question: A learner claims that light is necessary for starch production in a leaf. Outline a controlled test using a destarched plant, an opaque cover and iodine. State the expected result and one safety precaution.
theory.modelAnswer: Cover part of a leaf on a destarched plant with opaque material, leave another part exposed and place the plant in light. Test the leaf for starch after exposure. The exposed region should turn blue-black while the covered region remains yellow-brown. Heat ethanol in a water bath away from flames when removing chlorophyll.
markingPoints: Use a destarched plant with covered and exposed leaf regions. (2 marks)
Expose to light and describe starch testing with chlorophyll removal and iodine. (2 marks)
State the contrasting expected results. (2 marks)
State an appropriate ethanol/heating safety precaution. (1 mark)

theory.question: Explain how three features of a root hair cell support absorption from soil.
theory.modelAnswer: Its long extension increases contact surface area. Its thin wall offers a short path for water movement. A large vacuole containing cell sap can maintain a water-potential gradient for water entry under suitable soil conditions. Mitochondria can provide energy for active ion uptake.
markingPoints: First correct structure-function pair. (2 marks)
Second distinct structure-function pair. (2 marks)
Third distinct structure-function pair. (2 marks)

theory.question: Explain why a rise in blood glucose after a meal can trigger negative feedback. Refer to insulin and the subsequent change in glucose concentration.
theory.modelAnswer: Raised blood glucose stimulates insulin release from pancreatic beta cells. Insulin promotes glucose uptake by responsive tissues and storage, including glycogen formation. Blood glucose falls towards its regulated range, reducing the original stimulus for insulin release.
markingPoints: Identify the rise in glucose as a stimulus for insulin release. (2 marks)
Explain uptake or storage that lowers blood glucose. (2 marks)
Explain reduction of the original stimulus as glucose returns towards range. (2 marks)

theory.question: Distinguish seed dispersal from germination and explain two advantages that dispersal away from the parent may provide.
theory.modelAnswer: Dispersal moves seeds away from the parent; germination is the resumption of embryo growth under suitable conditions. Dispersal can reduce competition with the parent or siblings and allow colonisation of suitable new habitats.
markingPoints: Accurately distinguish dispersal from germination. (2 marks)
Explain one advantage. (2 marks)
Explain a second distinct advantage. (2 marks)

theory.question: In pea plants, R is completely dominant to r for the trait being studied. Cross Rr with rr. Give the possible gametes, expected offspring genotypes and expected dominant-to-recessive phenotype ratio.
theory.modelAnswer: Rr produces R and r gametes; rr produces r gametes. The expected offspring are half Rr and half rr, giving a 1:1 dominant-to-recessive phenotype ratio.
markingPoints: Correct gametes from both parents. (2 marks)
Correct offspring genotypes and equal expected proportions. (2 marks)
Correct phenotype ratio of 1:1. (1 mark)

theory.question: Five equal-area quadrats contain 4, 0, 3, 1 and 2 seedlings. Each quadrat covers 0.5 m². Estimate seedling density per square metre, and state one condition needed for a defensible estimate for the whole site.
theory.modelAnswer: There are 10 seedlings in 2.5 m², so estimated density is 4 seedlings per m². Quadrat placement should represent the site, for example through an appropriate random or stratified sampling design.
markingPoints: Find total count 10 and total sampled area 2.5 m². (2 marks)
Calculate 4 seedlings per m² with units. (2 marks)
State and explain representativeness of placement. (2 marks)

theory.question: A bacterial population contains a rare inherited resistance trait before exposure to an antibiotic. Explain how repeated exposure can increase the frequency of resistance without suggesting that the bacteria deliberately change.
theory.modelAnswer: Susceptible bacteria are more likely to be killed or prevented from reproducing. Resistant survivors reproduce and pass resistance to descendants, so their share of the population can rise. The treatment selects among existing heritable differences; it does not require purposeful change.
markingPoints: Use the initial inherited variation stated in the question. (1 mark)
Explain differential survival or reproduction during exposure. (2 marks)
Explain inheritance and increasing frequency over generations. (2 marks)
Reject purposeful change as the mechanism. (1 mark)

theory.question: Magnesium reacts according to 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Calculate the mass of MgO formed from 4.8 g Mg with excess oxygen. Use Mg = 24 and O = 16.
theory.modelAnswer: Amount of Mg = 4.8/24 = 0.20 mol. The equation gives the same amount of MgO. Molar mass MgO = 40 g mol⁻¹, so mass = 0.20×40 = 8.0 g.
markingPoints: Calculate 0.20 mol Mg. (2 marks)
Use the 1:1 Mg-to-MgO mole relationship. (1 mark)
Use molar mass 40 and obtain 8.0 g MgO. (2 marks)

theory.question: A solution contains 0.10 mol NaOH in 250 cm³. Find its concentration in mol dm⁻³ and the volume of 0.20 mol dm⁻³ HCl needed to neutralise the whole solution. Use HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.
theory.modelAnswer: 250 cm³ = 0.250 dm³. NaOH concentration = 0.10/0.250 = 0.40 mol dm⁻³. Neutralisation needs 0.10 mol HCl; volume = 0.10/0.20 = 0.50 dm³ = 500 cm³.
markingPoints: Convert solution volume to 0.250 dm³. (1 mark)
Calculate concentration 0.40 mol dm⁻³. (2 marks)
Apply 1:1 neutralisation to obtain 0.10 mol HCl. (1 mark)
Calculate 0.50 dm³ or 500 cm³ acid. (2 marks)

theory.question: In two experiments, equal masses of zinc react with equal volumes and concentrations of excess acid at different temperatures. The warmer experiment produces gas faster but gives the same final gas volume at the same measurement conditions. Explain both observations.
theory.modelAnswer: Higher temperature increases particle energies and the fraction of collisions exceeding activation energy, increasing rate. The same amount of limiting zinc reacts in each experiment, so the total amount of gas and its volume at equal measurement conditions are the same.
markingPoints: Relate temperature to particle energy and effective collisions. (3 marks)
Identify equal zinc amounts as the same limiting amount. (1 mark)
Connect equal gas moles with equal final volumes at common conditions. (2 marks)

theory.question: Distinguish a strong acid from a concentrated acid. Explain whether a dilute solution can contain a strong acid.
theory.modelAnswer: Strength concerns the extent of ionisation in water; concentration concerns the amount of acid per volume of solution. A strong acid such as HCl can be present in a dilute solution while the dissolved acid is still essentially fully ionised.
markingPoints: Define strength in terms of ionisation. (2 marks)
Define concentration as amount per volume. (2 marks)
Explain a dilute strong acid with a valid example. (2 marks)

theory.question: Iron objects rust more readily in moist air than in dry air. State the two conditions required for ordinary rusting and explain how an intact paint layer helps prevent it.
theory.modelAnswer: Ordinary rusting requires water and oxygen. An intact paint layer acts as a barrier that limits contact between the iron and both moisture and oxygen.
markingPoints: Identify water. (1 mark)
Identify oxygen. (1 mark)
Explain the physical barrier to contact. (2 marks)

theory.question: Describe a chemical test that distinguishes ethene from ethane under ordinary laboratory test conditions. State the reagent, contrasting observations and the reason.
theory.modelAnswer: Shake each gas with bromine water without ultraviolet light. Ethene decolourises it; ethane shows no rapid decolourisation under these conditions. Ethene undergoes addition at its carbon-carbon double bond, while ethane is saturated.
markingPoints: Identify bromine water with no ultraviolet light. (2 marks)
Give both contrasting observations. (2 marks)
Explain unsaturation and addition in ethene. (2 marks)

theory.question: A vehicle moving at 20 m s⁻¹ slows uniformly to rest in 5 s. Calculate its acceleration and stopping distance during braking.
theory.modelAnswer: Acceleration = (0−20)/5 = −4 m s⁻². Average velocity during uniform deceleration = (20+0)/2 = 10 m s⁻¹. Distance = 10×5 = 50 m.
markingPoints: Use velocity change over time and obtain −4 m s⁻². (2 marks)
Find average velocity or use an equivalent constant-acceleration relation. (1 mark)
Calculate 50 m with units. (2 marks)

theory.question: A 2 kg stone falls from rest through 5 m. Neglect air resistance and use g = 10 m s⁻². Find its loss of gravitational potential energy and its speed just before the end of the fall.
theory.modelAnswer: Potential-energy loss = mgh = 2×10×5 = 100 J. This becomes kinetic energy: ½×2×v² = 100, so v = 10 m s⁻¹.
markingPoints: Calculate 100 J gravitational energy lost. (2 marks)
Equate the energy to ½mv². (2 marks)
Obtain speed 10 m s⁻¹. (1 mark)

theory.question: Explain why coastal areas may experience a sea breeze during a sunny afternoon. Refer to differences in heating and air movement.
theory.modelAnswer: Land generally heats faster than the sea during the day. Air over the warmer land warms, expands and rises. Cooler, denser air from over the sea moves towards the land near the surface, forming the sea breeze and part of a convection circulation.
markingPoints: State faster daytime heating of land relative to sea. (2 marks)
Explain warmer air rising over land. (2 marks)
Explain near-surface replacement by air from the sea. (2 marks)

theory.question: A learner stands 85 m from a large wall and hears an echo. Taking sound speed as 340 m s⁻¹, calculate the time between the original sound and the echo. Explain why the travel distance is not 85 m.
theory.modelAnswer: The sound travels to the wall and back, a total of 170 m. Time = 170/340 = 0.50 s. The echo returns along a second 85 m path after reflection.
markingPoints: Identify the round-trip distance of 170 m. (2 marks)
Use t = distance/speed and obtain 0.50 s. (2 marks)
Explain the outward and reflected return paths. (1 mark)

theory.question: A 6 Ω resistor and a 3 Ω resistor are connected in parallel across an ideal 12 V supply. Calculate the current in each branch and the total power delivered to the pair.
theory.modelAnswer: The 6 Ω branch carries 12/6 = 2 A; the 3 Ω branch carries 12/3 = 4 A. Total current is 6 A, so power = 12×6 = 72 W.
markingPoints: Correct 2 A current in the 6 Ω branch. (2 marks)
Correct 4 A current in the 3 Ω branch. (2 marks)
Find total current 6 A and total power 72 W. (2 marks)

theory.question: A convex lens has focal length 10 cm. An object is placed 30 cm from the lens. Using 1/f = 1/u + 1/v for the real object and image distances here, calculate image distance and magnification, and describe the image.
theory.modelAnswer: 1/v = 1/10−1/30 = 1/15, so v = 15 cm. Magnification magnitude = v/u = 15/30 = 0.5. The image is real, inverted and diminished.
markingPoints: Substitute into the lens equation correctly. (2 marks)
Find image distance 15 cm. (1 mark)
Find magnification magnitude 0.5. (1 mark)
State real, inverted and diminished. (2 marks)

theory.question: Explain how transport, warehousing and banking can help a rice producer serve customers beyond the harvest area. Link each service to a distinct commercial barrier.
theory.modelAnswer: Transport moves rice to places where buyers need it, addressing distance. Warehousing holds rice between harvest and later sale, addressing timing. Banking can provide payment facilities or appropriate finance, helping exchange and funding needs.
markingPoints: Link transport to place/distance. (2 marks)
Link storage to time between production and consumption. (2 marks)
Link banking to payments or appropriate finance. (2 marks)

theory.question: Two skilled tailors plan to work together. Discuss two possible benefits of a partnership and two possible difficulties they should address before starting.
theory.modelAnswer: They can combine finance and complementary skills and share workload. They may disagree over decisions or contributions, and changes in one partner’s availability or willingness to continue can affect the business. A clear agreement on roles and financial arrangements can reduce avoidable uncertainty.
markingPoints: Explain two distinct benefits. (4 marks)
Explain two distinct difficulties. (4 marks)

theory.question: A remote farm sells a highly perishable crop. Compare direct sales to urban consumers with using a specialist distributor. Give one benefit and one limitation of each route, then state what evidence should guide the choice.
theory.modelAnswer: Direct sales may retain more of the selling price and provide customer contact, but require the farm to manage delivery and find customers. A distributor can provide established transport and market access, but charges a margin and may reduce the farmer’s control. Compare spoilage, delivery time, total costs, demand and achievable prices.
markingPoints: Benefit and limitation of direct selling. (4 marks)
Benefit and limitation of distributor use. (4 marks)
Identify relevant decision evidence. (2 marks)

theory.question: Distinguish an invoice, a receipt and a credit note. Use the case of a shop buying goods, paying the supplier and later returning an accepted damaged item.
theory.modelAnswer: The invoice states the goods supplied and amount charged. The receipt acknowledges payment. The supplier’s credit note records a reduction of the shop’s debt or a credit due for the accepted return.
markingPoints: Explain invoice using the sale. (2 marks)
Explain receipt using payment. (2 marks)
Explain credit note using the accepted return. (2 marks)

theory.question: A trader buys goods with a list price of ₦80,000 less a 10% trade discount. The invoice offers a further 2% cash discount on the discounted price for prompt payment. Calculate the invoice amount and prompt-payment amount, then distinguish the discounts.
theory.modelAnswer: Invoice amount = 80,000×0.90 = ₦72,000. Cash discount = 72,000×0.02 = ₦1,440; prompt payment = ₦70,560. Trade discount reduces the quoted list price; cash discount encourages payment within the stated period.
markingPoints: Calculate invoice amount ₦72,000. (2 marks)
Calculate cash discount ₦1,440 and payment ₦70,560. (2 marks)
Explain the different purposes. (2 marks)

theory.question: A bakery’s owner believes that buying fire insurance removes the need for fire prevention. Explain why this reasoning is unsound and give two prevention measures suitable for a bakery.
theory.modelAnswer: Insurance may compensate a covered financial loss within its terms, but cannot prevent injury, disruption or all uncovered costs. Prevention remains necessary. Suitable measures include maintaining electrical equipment, safe storage and handling of fuel, unobstructed exits and appropriate staff training.
markingPoints: Explain insurance’s limited financial role. (2 marks)
Explain a remaining human, operational or uncovered consequence. (2 marks)
Explain two suitable prevention measures. (4 marks)

theory.question: An online retailer has 120 orders recorded as dispatched, but only 95 delivery confirmations. Give two possible explanations and describe two records or checks needed before accusing a driver of theft.
theory.modelAnswer: Some parcels may still be in transit or awaiting confirmation, or there may be failed deliveries or recording errors. Reconcile parcel identifiers with carrier scans and delivery attempts, check proof-of-delivery records and contact customers or carriers through verified channels.
markingPoints: Explain two plausible causes other than assumed theft. (4 marks)
Describe two traceable reconciliation checks. (4 marks)

theory.question: A firm’s advertisement doubles visits to its website, but completed purchases do not rise. Explain why visits alone do not establish campaign success and give two further measures or investigations.
theory.modelAnswer: Visits show attention but not necessarily profitable sales. Examine conversion rates, order value, acquisition cost and repeat purchases. Investigate whether visitors face misleading offers, poor availability, delivery charges or checkout difficulty. Compare results with the campaign’s stated objective and cost.
markingPoints: Distinguish attention from purchases/profit. (2 marks)
Explain two useful measures or investigations. (4 marks)
Link judgement to objectives and costs. (2 marks)

theory.question: A purchasing officer can select suppliers, approve invoices and make payments without review. Explain two risks and propose two controls that preserve an audit trail.
theory.modelAnswer: Concentrating these duties creates opportunities for fictitious suppliers, inflated invoices or unnoticed errors. Separate ordering, approval and payment where possible, require evidence of receipt, use approval limits and retain dated records of who authorised each action.
markingPoints: Explain two distinct risks. (4 marks)
Explain two suitable controls linked to those risks. (4 marks)

theory.question: A shop’s staff receive conflicting instructions from two supervisors about the same delivery. Explain the management problem, one consequence and a practical way to resolve it.
theory.modelAnswer: Unclear authority or conflicting reporting lines cause the problem. Staff may duplicate work, miss deadlines or make inconsistent promises. Clarify who decides the delivery plan, document responsibilities and establish an agreed escalation route for conflicting instructions.
markingPoints: Identify conflicting authority/reporting responsibilities. (2 marks)
Explain a plausible operational consequence. (2 marks)
Propose clear responsibility and a communication/escalation process. (3 marks)

theory.question: The cash book shows a ₦20,000 debit bank balance. A bank charge of ₦1,000 and direct customer credit of ₦6,000 are unrecorded. The bank statement shows ₦22,000 positive balance; deposits in transit are ₦7,000 and unpresented cheques ₦4,000. Prepare the adjusted cash-book balance and reconcile it with the statement.
theory.modelAnswer: Adjusted cash book = 20,000−1,000+6,000 = ₦25,000 debit. Statement reconciliation: 22,000+7,000−4,000 = ₦25,000. Deposits in transit increase the statement balance when reconciling to the cash book; unpresented cheques reduce it.
markingPoints: Record charge as a reduction of bank by ₦1,000. (1 mark)
Record direct credit as an increase of ₦6,000. (1 mark)
Obtain adjusted balance ₦25,000 debit. (2 marks)
Add deposits in transit and subtract unpresented cheques from the positive statement balance. (2 marks)
Show agreement at ₦25,000. (1 mark)

theory.question: Prepare a short income calculation from these figures, all in naira: sales 200,000; sales returns 10,000; opening inventory 30,000; purchases 110,000; purchase returns 5,000; carriage inwards 5,000; closing inventory 40,000; wages paid 20,000 plus accrual 3,000; rent paid 12,000 including prepayment 2,000; depreciation 8,000. Find net sales, cost of sales, gross profit and net profit.
markingPoints: Calculate net sales 190,000. (1 mark)
Calculate cost of sales 100,000 with appropriate returns and inventory treatment. (3 marks)
Calculate gross profit 90,000. (1 mark)
Calculate wages 23,000 and rent 10,000. (2 marks)
Deduct depreciation and obtain net profit 49,000. (2 marks)

theory.question: An asset costs ₦100,000. Policy S depreciates it straight-line over four years with residual value ₦20,000. Policy R uses a 20% reducing-balance rate, with no residual-value constraint affecting the first two years. Calculate year-two depreciation and carrying amount after two years under each policy.
theory.modelAnswer: Policy S: annual depreciation = (100,000−20,000)/4 = ₦20,000; carrying amount after two years = ₦60,000. Policy R: first-year depreciation = ₦20,000, leaving ₦80,000; year-two depreciation = ₦16,000 and carrying amount = ₦64,000.
markingPoints: Find straight-line year-two expense 20,000. (2 marks)
Find straight-line carrying amount 60,000. (1 mark)
Find reducing-balance first-year carrying amount 80,000. (1 mark)
Find year-two expense 16,000 and final carrying amount 64,000. (3 marks)

theory.question: A club received subscriptions of ₦60,000. At the start of the year, subscriptions in arrears were ₦5,000 and in advance ₦4,000. At the end, arrears were ₦8,000 and advances ₦6,000. Find subscription income for the year and identify the closing balances as assets or liabilities.
theory.modelAnswer: Subscription income = 60,000−5,000+8,000+4,000−6,000 = ₦61,000. Closing arrears of ₦8,000 are a receivable asset, assuming recoverability; closing advances of ₦6,000 are a liability for the next membership period.
markingPoints: Remove opening arrears and add closing arrears. (2 marks)
Add opening advances and remove closing advances. (2 marks)
Calculate income 61,000. (1 mark)
Classify closing arrears and advances correctly. (2 marks)

theory.question: Prepare a manufacturing cost calculation from these figures in naira: opening raw materials 10,000; raw-material purchases 45,000; carriage inwards 2,000; closing raw materials 7,000; direct wages 30,000; direct expenses 5,000; factory overhead 20,000; opening work in progress 8,000; closing work in progress 6,000. Find raw materials consumed, prime cost and cost of production.
markingPoints: Calculate materials consumed 50,000. (2 marks)
Calculate prime cost 85,000. (2 marks)
Add factory overhead and correctly adjust work in progress. (2 marks)
Obtain production cost 107,000. (1 mark)

theory.question: A partnership earns ₦120,000 before appropriations. The agreement gives A a salary of ₦20,000, interest on capital of ₦10,000 to A and ₦6,000 to B, then shares the residual profit 3:2 between A and B. Find residual profit and each partner’s total entitlement. There are no other appropriations.
markingPoints: Calculate residual profit 84,000. (2 marks)
Allocate residual as 50,400 to A and 33,600 to B. (2 marks)
Find total A entitlement 80,400 and B entitlement 39,600. (2 marks)
Show allocation totals 120,000. (1 mark)

theory.question: Prepare the closing sales-ledger control balance from these naira figures: opening debit balance 40,000; credit sales 150,000; customer receipts 120,000; sales returns 8,000; discounts allowed 2,000; bad debts written off 3,000; dishonoured customer cheque 5,000. Assume no other entries and no opening credit balances.
theory.modelAnswer: Closing receivables = 40,000+150,000+5,000−120,000−8,000−2,000−3,000 = ₦62,000 debit. The dishonoured cheque restores the customer debt that the earlier receipt had reduced.
markingPoints: Include opening receivables and credit sales on the increasing side. (2 marks)
Add the dishonoured cheque correctly. (1 mark)
Deduct receipts, returns, discounts and bad debts. (3 marks)
Obtain 62,000 debit. (1 mark)

theory.question: A suspense account has a ₦6,000 debit balance. Investigation shows that a ₦10,000 credit purchase was correctly credited to the supplier but debited to purchases as ₦4,000. Separately, ₦3,000 of stationery was wrongly debited to rent, with the credit entry correct. Give the correcting journal entries and show which one clears suspense.
theory.modelAnswer: Debit purchases ₦6,000; credit suspense ₦6,000, clearing its debit balance. Separately, debit stationery ₦3,000; credit rent ₦3,000. The second correction does not involve suspense because its original debit and credit amounts balanced.
markingPoints: Calculate the missing purchase debit 6,000. (1 mark)
Correctly debit purchases and credit suspense by 6,000. (2 marks)
Show suspense cleared. (1 mark)
Correctly debit stationery and credit rent by 3,000 without suspense. (2 marks)

theory.question: Inventory consists of 10 units bought at ₦200 each and a later 20 units at ₦250 each. The business sells 18 units at ₦350 each. Under FIFO, calculate cost of sales, closing inventory and gross profit. Ignore other costs and returns.
theory.modelAnswer: FIFO issues the 10 earlier units costing ₦2,000 and 8 later units costing ₦2,000, so cost of sales is ₦4,000. Twelve later units remain at ₦250, giving closing inventory ₦3,000. Revenue is 18×350 = ₦6,300, so gross profit is ₦2,300.
markingPoints: Allocate 10 units from the first batch and 8 from the second. (2 marks)
Calculate cost of sales 4,000. (1 mark)
Calculate closing inventory 3,000. (2 marks)
Calculate revenue 6,300 and gross profit 2,300. (2 marks)

theory.question: Opening assets are ₦180,000 and liabilities ₦40,000. Closing assets are ₦250,000 and liabilities ₦70,000. During the year the proprietor introduced ₦20,000 capital and withdrew ₦30,000. Use the capital comparison method to calculate profit, assuming no other equity changes.
markingPoints: Calculate opening capital 140,000. (1 mark)
Calculate closing capital 180,000. (1 mark)
Adjust correctly for drawings and introduced capital. (2 marks)
Obtain profit 50,000. (1 mark)

theory.question: A state has a detailed written constitution, but officials routinely ignore court orders and approved procedures. Explain why having a written constitution is not sufficient to establish constitutionalism. Give three supporting conditions.
theory.modelAnswer: Constitutionalism means public power is exercised within effective limits, not merely that a document exists. Relevant conditions include enforceable rules and court decisions, independent oversight, transparent procedures, public access to remedies and a political culture of compliance.
markingPoints: Distinguish a constitutional document from effective limitation of power. (3 marks)
Explain three supporting conditions. (6 marks)

theory.question: Explain three safeguards that can support judicial independence and one reason why independence should coexist with proper accountability.
theory.modelAnswer: Safeguards include a transparent merit-based appointment process, secure tenure with due removal procedures, adequate protected administration and freedom from improper pressure in deciding cases. Accountability is needed to address misconduct or incompetence through fair processes without dictating judgments.
markingPoints: Explain three distinct safeguards. (6 marks)
Explain a proper accountability purpose and its limits. (3 marks)

theory.question: Compare a federal distribution of power with a unitary arrangement in responding to a disaster that affects several regions. Give one coordination benefit and one possible difficulty for each.
theory.modelAnswer: Federal arrangements can allow regional responses informed by local conditions but may require coordination across constitutionally divided responsibilities. A unitary arrangement can coordinate national direction through a common authority but may overlook local needs or face administrative bottlenecks. Actual performance depends on capacity and institutional design.
markingPoints: Explain the basic difference in allocation of authority. (2 marks)
Benefit and difficulty of federal response. (4 marks)
Benefit and difficulty of unitary response. (4 marks)

theory.question: In a hypothetical election there are 2,000 registered voters. Valid votes are 720 for A and 680 for B; 50 ballots are invalid. Calculate turnout and A’s percentage of valid votes, to one decimal place. Explain why the two denominators differ.
theory.modelAnswer: Ballots cast = 720+680+50 = 1,450. Turnout = 1,450/2,000×100 = 72.5%. A’s valid-vote share = 720/1,400×100 ≈ 51.4%. Turnout uses all ballots cast relative to registered voters; candidate share uses valid votes only.
markingPoints: Find 1,450 ballots cast. (1 mark)
Calculate turnout 72.5%. (2 marks)
Use 1,400 valid votes and obtain about 51.4%. (2 marks)
Explain the different denominators. (2 marks)

theory.question: An environmental association wants stricter waste controls but does not seek governmental office. Explain why it is a pressure group, describe two legitimate methods it can use and identify one limitation of its claim to represent the public.
theory.modelAnswer: Its central aim is policy influence rather than winning office. It can submit research to hearings, petition representatives, organise lawful campaigns or negotiate with agencies. Its members may not represent every affected resident, so transparent membership and evidence are important.
markingPoints: Apply the pressure-group distinction to the association. (2 marks)
Explain two legitimate methods. (4 marks)
Explain one limitation of representativeness. (2 marks)

theory.question: A senior official is instructed to direct routine public services only to supporters of the governing party. Explain how professional neutrality, equal treatment and accountability are relevant, and propose an appropriate institutional response in this hypothetical case.
theory.modelAnswer: Professional neutrality requires administration based on lawful public duties rather than party favour. Equal treatment requires relevant service criteria rather than political support. The official should use established clarification, reporting and review channels, preserve an accurate record and seek lawful resolution rather than secretly falsify records.
markingPoints: Explain neutrality. (2 marks)
Explain equal service treatment. (2 marks)
Explain a documented lawful reporting/review response. (3 marks)

theory.question: Explain why a colonial policy of indirect rule could produce different results in areas with centralised traditional authority and areas with several dispersed decision-making institutions. Include one possible consequence of appointing an intermediary without local legitimacy.
theory.modelAnswer: Existing central authorities could provide established channels for administration, although acceptance was not guaranteed. In decentralised settings, a single appointed intermediary could conflict with assemblies or other institutions. An appointee lacking legitimacy might face resistance, weaken existing checks or create new concentrations of power.
markingPoints: Explain use of established central authority. (2 marks)
Explain difficulties where authority was dispersed. (3 marks)
Explain one consequence of an unaccepted intermediary. (3 marks)

theory.question: Discuss how newspapers, organised labour and educated associations could contribute to anti-colonial nationalism in West Africa. Explain why none alone should be treated as the sole cause of independence.
theory.modelAnswer: Newspapers circulated criticism and political ideas; organised labour mobilised collective demands and action; educated associations developed programmes, leaders and networks. Their effects interacted with wider social, economic and international changes, and independence followed different processes across territories.
markingPoints: Explain the role of newspapers. (2 marks)
Explain the role of labour. (2 marks)
Explain the role of educated associations. (2 marks)
Explain interaction with other causes and local variation. (2 marks)

theory.question: A local council plans a market project. Residents want to know who selected the contractor and whether the promised work was delivered. Describe four accountability arrangements that would help answer these questions.
theory.modelAnswer: Use documented selection criteria, record conflicts and approvals, publish an understandable project budget, retain invoices and payment records, inspect work against agreed milestones and provide an accessible complaint channel. Together these connect decisions, expenditure and results.
markingPoints: Explain four suitable arrangements, each linked to a decision, payment or delivered result. (8 marks)

theory.question: A hypothetical state wants cheaper imports from a distant partner, stronger relations with neighbours and protection of local jobs. Explain three considerations its foreign-policy makers should weigh and why the goals may involve trade-offs.
theory.modelAnswer: They should consider economic gains and adjustment costs, regional commitments and relations, security and diplomatic interests, and the distribution of benefits and losses at home. Cheaper imports may help consumers while competing with some producers; a distant agreement may affect regional partners. The choice requires evidence and negotiation rather than assuming all goals improve simultaneously.
markingPoints: Explain three relevant considerations. (6 marks)
Explain a concrete trade-off between goals. (3 marks)

theory.question: On a hypothetical square grid, A is at easting 10 km and northing 20 km; B is at easting 14 km and northing 23 km. Find the straight-line distance AB and its general compass direction from A. Explain why a road journey can be longer.
theory.modelAnswer: The eastward change is 4 km and northward change 3 km. AB = √(4²+3²) = 5 km, generally north-east. A road may bend around terrain, property or rivers rather than follow the straight line.
markingPoints: Find east/north differences of 4 km and 3 km. (2 marks)
Use Pythagoras to obtain 5 km. (2 marks)
State north-east. (1 mark)
Explain a plausible reason for a longer route. (2 marks)

theory.question: Route P climbs from 120 m to 320 m over a horizontal distance of 2 km. Route Q reaches the same endpoints over 5 km. Calculate each average gradient as 1:n and explain one benefit and one cost of choosing the gentler route for a road.
theory.modelAnswer: The rise is 200 m. P has gradient 200/2,000 = 1:10; Q has gradient 200/5,000 = 1:25. Q is gentler, which may ease climbing and reduce steep-slope engineering demands, but its greater length can raise construction, travel or land-use costs.
markingPoints: Calculate rise 200 m. (1 mark)
Calculate P as 1:10. (2 marks)
Calculate Q as 1:25. (2 marks)
Explain one benefit and one cost of Q. (4 marks)

theory.question: A hypothetical station has monthly rainfall (mm) Jan–Dec: 24, 30, 62, 120, 180, 220, 240, 220, 180, 110, 50, 25. Monthly mean temperatures (°C) are 25, 26, 27, 28, 27, 26, 25, 25, 26, 26, 25, 24. Calculate annual rainfall and annual temperature range. Identify months with rainfall strictly below 50 mm and describe the seasonal pattern.
theory.modelAnswer: Annual rainfall totals 1,461 mm. Temperature range is 28−24 = 4°C. January, February and December are below 50 mm; November equals 50 and is excluded. Rain is concentrated in the middle of the year while temperatures remain high with a small annual range.
markingPoints: Calculate annual rainfall 1,461 mm. (2 marks)
Calculate temperature range 4°C. (1 mark)
Identify Jan, Feb and Dec only. (2 marks)
Describe the wet-season concentration and limited temperature variation. (3 marks)

theory.question: A river cross-section has width 8 m and mean depth 0.75 m. Mean velocity is 1.2 m s⁻¹. Estimate discharge and explain two reasons why one such estimate may not represent the river throughout the year.
theory.modelAnswer: Area ≈ 8×0.75 = 6 m². Discharge = 6×1.2 = 7.2 m³ s⁻¹. Rainfall, season and recent storms can change water level and velocity; one measurement may also miss spatial variation or measurement error. Repeat measurements at suitable times and use representative depth and velocity observations.
markingPoints: Calculate cross-sectional area 6 m². (2 marks)
Calculate discharge 7.2 m³ s⁻¹. (2 marks)
Explain two distinct temporal or measurement limitations. (4 marks)

theory.question: Plan a fair investigation comparing daytime air temperature in a paved town centre and a vegetated rural site. State three conditions or methods to standardise and explain why repeated observations are useful.
theory.modelAnswer: Use comparable calibrated instruments and shielding, the same height above ground and matched observation times. Avoid placing one sensor in direct sun while the other is shaded differently by its housing. Repeat on several days and at several representative sites to distinguish persistent patterns from a single weather event or site peculiarity.
markingPoints: State and explain three suitable standardised methods or conditions. (6 marks)
Explain why repeats across time or sites improve interpretation. (2 marks)

theory.question: A hypothetical district begins the year with 100,000 residents. During the year there are 4,200 births, 1,800 deaths, 900 immigrants and 600 emigrants. Calculate natural increase, net migration, total population change and percentage growth on the opening population.
theory.modelAnswer: Natural increase = 4,200−1,800 = 2,400. Net migration = 900−600 = 300. Total change = 2,700, giving 2.7% growth relative to 100,000. Closing population is 102,700 if these are the only changes.
markingPoints: Calculate natural increase 2,400. (1 mark)
Calculate net migration 300. (1 mark)
Calculate total change 2,700. (2 marks)
Calculate growth 2.7%. (2 marks)

theory.question: For a hypothetical factory, unit costs in naira are: Site P—raw-material delivery 4,000, outward delivery 2,000, labour 3,000, energy 1,000; Site Q—7,000, 1,000, 2,000 and 1,000 respectively. Calculate total unit cost at each site, choose the lower-cost site using only the table and explain two other factors needed before a final location decision.
theory.modelAnswer: P totals ₦10,000 per unit; Q totals ₦11,000. P is lower by ₦1,000 on these figures. Reliability of energy and transport, market access, land conditions, environmental impacts or future expansion can affect the final decision.
markingPoints: Calculate P cost 10,000. (1 mark)
Calculate Q cost 11,000. (1 mark)
Select P and state the 1,000 difference. (2 marks)
Explain two additional relevant locational factors. (4 marks)

theory.question: After extensive vegetation clearance in a catchment, a similar storm is followed by a faster river rise and muddier water. Explain two mechanisms that could connect clearance with these observations, and one reason why the comparison alone does not prove clearance was the only cause.
theory.modelAnswer: Reduced interception and infiltration can increase rapid surface runoff, shortening the response time. Less protective cover and root binding can increase soil erosion, adding sediment. Soil moisture before the storm, drainage works or differences in rainfall intensity could also affect the observations.
markingPoints: Explain faster runoff through reduced interception/infiltration. (3 marks)
Explain erosion and increased sediment. (3 marks)
Identify and explain a relevant alternative factor. (2 marks)

theory.question: A coastal community plans to expand tourism. Discuss two possible local benefits, two pressures on the community or environment and two management measures linked to those pressures.
theory.modelAnswer: Benefits can include jobs and income for local suppliers. Pressures can include waste, water demand, habitat damage, congestion or higher seasonal living costs. Suitable measures include reliable waste systems, water-use planning, habitat protection, visitor-capacity management and opportunities for local participation.
markingPoints: Explain two benefits. (4 marks)
Explain two distinct pressures. (4 marks)
Explain two measures linked to pressures. (4 marks)

theory.question: Compare how water conditions can influence settlement and transport in a low-lying Niger Delta wetland area and a much drier northern Nigerian savanna area. Give two influences for each and one caution against overgeneralising.
theory.modelAnswer: In a wetland delta, channels may support water transport while flooding and waterlogged ground complicate roads and building. In a drier savanna area, settlements may cluster near reliable water and seasonal shortages may constrain farming or water supply. Conditions vary within each region, and infrastructure or technology can modify the effects.
markingPoints: Explain two water-related influences in the delta setting. (4 marks)
Explain two in the drier savanna setting. (4 marks)
State and explain local variation or human adaptation. (2 marks)

theory.question: A settled soil sample forms layers 5 cm sand, 3 cm silt and 2 cm clay. Treat layer depth as proportional to fraction quantity for this classroom estimate. Calculate each percentage and explain one limitation of inferring field drainage from these readings alone.
theory.modelAnswer: Total depth = 10 cm. Sand is 50%, silt 30% and clay 20%. Field drainage also depends on structure, compaction, organic matter and other conditions; settling behaviour may not perfectly represent particle mass fractions.
markingPoints: Calculate sand 50%. (1 mark)
Calculate silt 30%. (1 mark)
Calculate clay 20%. (1 mark)
Explain a field-property or measurement limitation. (2 marks)

theory.question: A crop’s stated suitable soil-pH range is 6–7. Plot A has pH 4.5 and plot B pH 6.5. Select the plot that already meets the range. Explain why any treatment of A should follow soil assessment rather than assuming the same lime quantity for every field.
theory.modelAnswer: B already meets the stated range. A is more acidic, but a suitable amendment requirement depends on soil properties, buffering and the crop’s needs. Soil assessment should guide the choice and quantity; applying a universal amount may be ineffective or excessive.
markingPoints: Select B using the given range. (2 marks)
Identify A as more acidic. (1 mark)
Explain variation in amendment requirement and need for assessment. (3 marks)

theory.question: For a hypothetical calculation, a field is 0.4 ha and its assessed requirement is 60 kg nitrogen per hectare. The only planned nitrogen source is fertiliser containing 20% nitrogen by mass. Calculate the required nitrogen and corresponding fertiliser mass. Ignore other nutrient sources.
theory.modelAnswer: Nitrogen requirement = 0.4×60 = 24 kg. At 20% nitrogen, fertiliser mass = 24/0.20 = 120 kg.
markingPoints: Calculate 24 kg nitrogen for the field. (2 marks)
Convert 20% to a mass fraction and divide appropriately. (2 marks)
Obtain 120 kg fertiliser. (1 mark)

theory.question: A germination test of 100 seeds produces 84 normal seedlings, 8 abnormal seedlings and 8 ungerminated seeds. Using normal seedlings as the criterion, calculate germination percentage. Estimate how many seeds would be needed for an expected 420 normal seedlings at that rate, and explain why field establishment may differ.
theory.modelAnswer: Germination percentage = 84%. Expected seed requirement = 420/0.84 = 500. Field establishment can differ because of moisture, temperature, pests, planting depth and losses after germination. The estimate is an expectation, not a guarantee for each lot of 500.
markingPoints: Calculate 84%. (2 marks)
Calculate expected requirement 500 seeds. (2 marks)
Explain relevant field differences or sampling uncertainty. (3 marks)

theory.question: A monitoring protocol says intervention should be considered when at least 30% of sampled plants show a specified pest damage. A representative sample has 20 damaged plants out of 100 and many natural enemies. Explain the threshold result and two sensible next management steps without assuming a particular chemical treatment.
theory.modelAnswer: Observed damage is 20%, below the stated 30% threshold. Continue representative monitoring and confirm the pest, crop stage and damage trend. Preserve useful natural enemies and consider appropriate preventive or non-chemical measures. The result does not justify ignoring a rising problem or automatically applying a pesticide.
markingPoints: Calculate or identify 20% and compare correctly with 30%. (2 marks)
Explain continued monitoring and pest/damage confirmation. (3 marks)
Explain a relevant natural-enemy or preventive step. (2 marks)

theory.question: A farm’s tractor maintenance record shows frequent breakdowns after scheduled servicing was skipped. Explain two reasons for preventive maintenance and describe three useful items to record for each service.
theory.modelAnswer: Preventive maintenance can detect wear before failure and support reliable, safer operation. Records can include date and operating hours, work completed and parts used, faults identified, technician identity and the next service due.
markingPoints: Explain two maintenance benefits. (4 marks)
Describe three useful service-record items. (3 marks)

theory.question: A farmer buys animals from another herd. Explain why immediate unrestricted mixing can be risky even when no obvious illness is visible, and describe three general biosecurity arrangements to discuss with a qualified animal-health professional.
theory.modelAnswer: Some infections or parasites may not cause obvious signs immediately. Suitable arrangements can include separate observation facilities, verified health and movement records, controlled equipment and visitor contact, and a professionally planned health assessment.
markingPoints: Explain possible unobserved infection or incubation. (2 marks)
Explain three appropriate general biosecurity arrangements. (6 marks)

theory.question: Two groups of the same livestock breed grow at different rates, but one receives better feed and is older at weighing. Explain why the comparison does not establish genetic superiority and outline a fairer performance comparison.
theory.modelAnswer: Age and feeding differ, so growth differences cannot be attributed to genetics alone. Compare animals at matched ages and under comparable feeding, health and management, use suitable group sizes and repeated records, and assess traits relevant to the breeding objective.
markingPoints: Identify age and feeding as confounders. (2 marks)
Describe matched age and feeding/management. (3 marks)
Explain adequate records, groups or repeat assessment. (2 marks)

theory.question: In a hypothetical pond, dissolved oxygen is 2 mg L⁻¹ near dawn and 7 mg L⁻¹ in the afternoon. Fish show surface-gasping behaviour near dawn. Explain a possible daily biological mechanism, one further check and one general management response for low oxygen.
theory.modelAnswer: Photosynthesis can raise oxygen during daylight, while respiration continues at night without photosynthesis. Check oxygen measurements and other water conditions rather than assume one symptom proves the cause. Appropriate aeration and review of stocking, feeding and organic loading can form part of management.
markingPoints: Explain daytime photosynthesis and night respiration. (3 marks)
Describe a relevant measurement or water-quality check. (2 marks)
Explain a suitable general response such as aeration or reviewing loading. (2 marks)

theory.question: A farm enterprise earns ₦300,000 revenue, incurs ₦180,000 variable cost and ₦50,000 fixed cost. Calculate gross margin and net profit under these definitions. If revenue falls by 10% while costs stay unchanged, calculate the new net profit and explain the risk shown.
theory.modelAnswer: Gross margin = 300,000−180,000 = ₦120,000. Net profit = 120,000−50,000 = ₦70,000. New revenue = ₦270,000 and new net profit = ₦40,000. A 10% revenue fall reduces profit by ₦30,000, illustrating sensitivity when costs do not adjust.
markingPoints: Calculate gross margin 120,000. (1 mark)
Calculate original net profit 70,000. (1 mark)
Calculate new revenue 270,000 and profit 40,000. (3 marks)
Explain profit sensitivity under unchanged costs. (2 marks)

theory.question: Trace this pseudocode and give x and total after each iteration: x←1; total←0; WHILE x<5: total←total+2*x; x←x+1; END WHILE. State final output total and explain what happens if the x increment is removed.
theory.modelAnswer: After successive iterations, (x,total) is (2,2), (3,6), (4,12), (5,20). Final total is 20. Without the increment, x remains 1, the condition stays true and the loop does not terminate under the stated model.
markingPoints: Correct four successive state pairs. (4 marks)
Final total 20. (1 mark)
Explain unchanged x and non-termination if the increment is removed. (3 marks)

theory.question: Construct the complete truth table for a two-input NAND gate and explain how its result differs from AND. Use inputs 00, 01, 10 and 11.
theory.modelAnswer: For 00 the output is 1; for 01 it is 1; for 10 it is 1; for 11 it is 0. NAND is the negation of AND, so it gives the opposite binary output for every input pair.
markingPoints: Correct output for each of four input pairs. (4 marks)
Explain negation of AND. (2 marks)

theory.question: A spreadsheet has daily pay in B2 and days worked in C2. A fixed bonus rate is stored in F1. Write a formula in D2 for B2*C2 plus a bonus equal to that product multiplied by F1. Make F1 stay fixed when copied down, and give the resulting formula in D3.
theory.modelAnswer: D2: =B2*C2*(1+$F$1). Copied to D3: =B3*C3*(1+$F$1). Equivalent formulas that add the base pay and bonus separately are also valid.
markingPoints: Correct base-pay product. (1 mark)
Correct bonus application and total. (2 marks)
Use an absolute reference for F1. (2 marks)
Give the correct copied row-3 formula. (2 marks)

theory.question: A school stores learner details repeatedly in every subject-result row. A phone number is changed in some rows but not others. Explain the problem and propose a simpler linked-table design using a unique learner identifier.
theory.modelAnswer: Repeated learner details create redundancy and update anomalies. Store one learner row per unique learner identifier with the contact details, and store subject results separately with a reference to that identifier. Updating the learner contact once then avoids inconsistent copies in result rows.
markingPoints: Explain redundancy and inconsistent updates. (3 marks)
Propose a learner table with unique identifier. (2 marks)
Propose linked result rows and explain the single update benefit. (3 marks)

theory.question: A shared folder is synchronised to another device. A user accidentally deletes files and the deletion synchronises too. Explain why synchronisation alone was insufficient and describe two recovery safeguards.
theory.modelAnswer: Synchronisation can copy changes, including deletion, rather than preserve an independent earlier state. Use versioned backups with suitable retention and a protected separate copy, and test restoring required files. Access controls and recovery records help prevent or investigate further loss.
markingPoints: Explain propagation of deletion. (2 marks)
Explain two suitable safeguards linked to recoverable earlier states or protection. (4 marks)
Explain a restore test or retained recovery evidence. (2 marks)

theory.question: A computer can reach a known local service by IP address but cannot resolve its hostname. Other conditions are unchanged. Identify a likely area to investigate and describe a sensible check before replacing hardware.
theory.modelAnswer: Investigate name resolution, including the configured DNS service or local name records. Compare a known correct hostname, check relevant settings and test whether other names resolve. Since IP access works, a complete physical-network failure is not established.
markingPoints: Identify name-resolution/DNS investigation. (2 marks)
Describe two relevant checks or comparisons. (4 marks)
Explain why successful IP access weakens a total hardware-failure claim. (2 marks)

theory.question: A raw uncompressed image is 100 pixels wide and 80 pixels high at 8 bits per pixel. Ignoring headers and palettes, calculate size in bits, bytes and KiB, where 1 KiB=1024 bytes. Explain why an actual saved file may have a different size.
theory.modelAnswer: Size = 100×80×8 = 64,000 bits = 8,000 bytes = 7.8125 KiB. Headers, palettes, metadata or compression can change the saved file size relative to the raw pixel-data calculation.
markingPoints: Calculate 64,000 bits. (1 mark)
Convert to 8,000 bytes. (1 mark)
Convert to 7.8125 KiB. (2 marks)
Explain a valid file-format or compression difference. (2 marks)

theory.question: A long school report has manually enlarged headings, repeated blank lines and inconsistent page starts. Explain how paragraph styles, proper page breaks and an automatic contents feature could improve maintainability.
theory.modelAnswer: Styles apply consistent heading formatting and document structure. Proper page breaks control new pages without fragile runs of blank lines. Heading-based contents can be updated when sections or pagination change.
markingPoints: Explain styles and consistent structured headings. (2 marks)
Explain stable page breaks. (2 marks)
Explain an updateable contents list. (2 marks)

theory.question: Design tests for a score input that must be an integer from 0 to 100 inclusive. Give one ordinary valid value, both valid endpoints, one value below range, one above range and a non-integer input. State expected acceptance or rejection and why these tests are not proof of the whole program’s correctness.
theory.modelAnswer: Examples: 50 accepted; 0 accepted; 100 accepted; −1 rejected; 101 rejected; 1.5 or non-numeric text rejected. These check representative type/range and boundary behaviour but do not test every processing path, storage action or output elsewhere in the program.
markingPoints: Ordinary valid value and both accepted endpoints. (3 marks)
Rejected below-range, above-range and non-integer cases. (3 marks)
Explain a limitation of the test set. (2 marks)

theory.question: A staff member needs a list of learners eligible for a club, but requests an unrestricted export containing home addresses and unrelated family details. Explain two privacy or access concerns and propose a proportionate information-sharing approach.
theory.modelAnswer: The export includes more personal information than needed and may give access beyond the staff member’s role. Provide only authorised fields relevant to eligibility, apply appropriate access controls and retain a record of the approved purpose and disclosure.
markingPoints: Explain excess/unnecessary data concern. (2 marks)
Explain role or access-authorisation concern. (2 marks)
Propose a relevant minimal authorised dataset and traceable sharing arrangement. (3 marks)

theory.question: Assess the value and limitations of oral traditions for reconstructing early Nigerian history. Develop four points and explain how corroboration improves the investigation.
theory.modelAnswer: Indicative response: Oral traditions can preserve genealogies, migration narratives and memories omitted from surviving written records. Performance, audience and later political interests can reshape a remembered account, so versions and context should be recorded. Generational sequences may be informative without supplying precise calendar dates; avoid assigning fixed lengths mechanically. Compare independent versions with archaeology, linguistics and dated records; agreement strengthens a claim while contradictions require explanation.
markingPoints: Point 1: Oral traditions can preserve genealogies, migration narratives and memories omitted from surviving written records. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 2: Performance, audience and later political interests can reshape a remembered account, so versions and context should be recorded. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 3: Generational sequences may be informative without supplying precise calendar dates; avoid assigning fixed lengths mechanically. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 4: Compare independent versions with archaeology, linguistics and dated records; agreement strengthens a claim while contradictions require explanation. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

theory.question: Explain four ways material remains can illuminate early Nigerian societies, while acknowledging one limit of such evidence.
theory.modelAnswer: Indicative response: Tools and workshop waste can indicate production techniques and occupational specialisation. Burial goods and settlement layouts can suggest social distinctions, but status interpretations need contextual support. Non-local materials can indicate exchange networks, though an imported object alone does not prove foreign settlement. Objects rarely reveal a complete political narrative by themselves; use secure contexts and corroborating sources.
markingPoints: Point 1: Tools and workshop waste can indicate production techniques and occupational specialisation. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 2: Burial goods and settlement layouts can suggest social distinctions, but status interpretations need contextual support. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 3: Non-local materials can indicate exchange networks, though an imported object alone does not prove foreign settlement. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 4: Objects rarely reveal a complete political narrative by themselves; use secure contexts and corroborating sources. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

theory.question: Discuss how craft specialisation and markets could promote relations between precolonial Nigerian communities. Develop four explained links.
theory.modelAnswer: Indicative response: Specialist smiths supplied tools that farming households needed, creating regular exchange. Food producers supplied grain and other provisions to craftspeople whose time was concentrated on production. Market meetings enabled information exchange and relationships beyond the immediate settlement. Repeated exchange could encourage negotiated security and routes, although competition and disputes could also arise.
markingPoints: Point 1: Specialist smiths supplied tools that farming households needed, creating regular exchange. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 2: Food producers supplied grain and other provisions to craftspeople whose time was concentrated on production. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 3: Market meetings enabled information exchange and relationships beyond the immediate settlement. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 4: Repeated exchange could encourage negotiated security and routes, although competition and disputes could also arise. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

theory.question: Explain four ways trans-Saharan commerce could influence West African societies. Avoid treating every region as affected identically.
theory.modelAnswer: Indicative response: Caravan trade linked production areas with distant demand and could support towns at route junctions. Rulers could obtain revenue by taxing commerce, strengthening some political centres. Merchants and scholars facilitated Islamic learning and religious contacts, though adoption varied. Imported goods and changing demand influenced consumption and production; access and benefits differed by location and social group.
markingPoints: Point 1: Caravan trade linked production areas with distant demand and could support towns at route junctions. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 2: Rulers could obtain revenue by taxing commerce, strengthening some political centres. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 3: Merchants and scholars facilitated Islamic learning and religious contacts, though adoption varied. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 4: Imported goods and changing demand influenced consumption and production; access and benefits differed by location and social group. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

theory.question: Evaluate the claim that replacing slave exports with commodity exports meant all labour in nineteenth-century West African production immediately became free. Develop four points.
theory.modelAnswer: Indicative response: The phrase legitimate commerce distinguished commodity exports from trading enslaved people; it did not describe every labour relationship. Palm produce and other exports could expand while coerced labour persisted in some settings. Suppressing oceanic slave trading differed from emancipating people already held in slavery. A defensible conclusion requires local evidence on labour status and enforcement rather than inferring universal freedom from export categories.
markingPoints: Point 1: The phrase legitimate commerce distinguished commodity exports from trading enslaved people; it did not describe every labour relationship. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 2: Palm produce and other exports could expand while coerced labour persisted in some settings. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 3: Suppressing oceanic slave trading differed from emancipating people already held in slavery. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 4: A defensible conclusion requires local evidence on labour status and enforcement rather than inferring universal freedom from export categories. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

theory.question: A proposed history says: “Colonial railways benefited every Nigerian district equally.” Assess this claim through four lines of investigation.
theory.modelAnswer: Indicative response: Map routes against produce districts and ports to identify export priorities and places bypassed. Compare freight charges and transport access to examine how gains differed between users and regions. Investigate labour recruitment, land acquisition and associated costs rather than considering benefits alone. Use local income and market evidence over time; route construction alone cannot establish equal welfare gains.
markingPoints: Point 1: Map routes against produce districts and ports to identify export priorities and places bypassed. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 2: Compare freight charges and transport access to examine how gains differed between users and regions. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 3: Investigate labour recruitment, land acquisition and associated costs rather than considering benefits alone. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 4: Use local income and market evidence over time; route construction alone cannot establish equal welfare gains. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

theory.question: Explain why the expansion of mission schooling did not produce identical educational experiences throughout colonial Nigeria. Develop four points.
theory.modelAnswer: Indicative response: Mission activity and school locations differed across regions and communities. Household resources, fees and travel distances influenced attendance. Gender expectations and local preferences could shape access and subjects studied. Government policies, religious concerns and existing learning institutions affected local responses; schooling expanded unevenly rather than replacing all earlier learning.
markingPoints: Point 1: Mission activity and school locations differed across regions and communities. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)
Point 2: Household resources, fees and travel distances influenced attendance. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 3: Gender expectations and local preferences could shape access and subjects studied. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 4: Government policies, religious concerns and existing learning institutions affected local responses; schooling expanded unevenly rather than replacing all earlier learning. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

theory.question: How can historians investigate colonial-era women’s political action without relying only on official descriptions of disorder? Develop four explained methods.
theory.modelAnswer: Indicative response: Collect participants’ and community accounts, while checking memory and the circumstances of recording. Examine petitions, songs and meeting records to identify demands and organisation. Read official reports critically for administrative interests, omissions and language. Compare independent sources and local economic conditions to reconstruct motives and action; avoid assuming one motive for every participant.
markingPoints: Point 1: Collect participants’ and community accounts, while checking memory and the circumstances of recording. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 2: Examine petitions, songs and meeting records to identify demands and organisation. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 3: Read official reports critically for administrative interests, omissions and language. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

Point 4: Compare independent sources and local economic conditions to reconstruct motives and action; avoid assuming one motive for every participant. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

theory.question: Distinguish political independence from economic independence in interpreting Nigeria after 1960. Develop four connected points.
theory.modelAnswer: Indicative response: Political independence transferred sovereign governmental authority from colonial rule. Economic dependence can persist through reliance on imported manufactures, finance or a narrow export base. Changes in overseas commodity prices can constrain revenue despite formal sovereignty. Assess diversification, domestic production and distribution with evidence rather than treating constitutional independence as proof of equal prosperity.
markingPoints: Point 1: Political independence transferred sovereign governmental authority from colonial rule. Award 1 mark for the relevant point and 1 for a historically sound explanation or supporting example. (2 marks)

theory.question: Distinguish physical reconstruction from social reintegration after the Nigerian Civil War. Explain why a historian should investigate both, using four developed points.

theory.question: En environ 100 mots, racontez une activité collective à laquelle vous avez participé dans votre quartier. Présentez la situation initiale, les actions, le résultat et ce que vous avez appris.
theory.modelAnswer: Dans notre quartier, une petite place était souvent couverte de papiers et de sacs usagés. Samedi dernier, mes amis et moi avons décidé de la nettoyer avec quelques adultes. Nous avons d’abord demandé des gants et des sacs solides. Ensuite, nous avons ramassé les déchets sans toucher aux objets dangereux, que les adultes ont signalés au service compétent. Pendant le travail, une voisine nous a apporté de l’eau. À la fin de la matinée, la place était plus agréable. Cependant, un nettoyage ne suffit pas. Nous souhaitons maintenant installer des poubelles et expliquer aux habitants comment garder cet espace propre. Cette expérience m’a appris qu’une action collective doit être suivie d’efforts réguliers.

theory.modelAnswer:
Chère Aïcha,
J’espère que tu vas bien. Je t’écris pour t’inviter à la journée de lecture que notre école organise samedi prochain. La rencontre commencera à neuf heures dans la salle principale. Chaque participant pourra présenter un livre qu’il a aimé, puis écouter les autres. Tu n’es pas obligée d’apporter un livre neuf : un ouvrage emprunté convient aussi. Après les présentations, nous discuterons en petits groupes et échangerons des conseils de lecture. Je pense que cette activité te plaira, car tu racontes toujours les histoires avec beaucoup d’enthousiasme. Si tu es libre, réponds-moi avant jeudi pour que je réserve une place. Je pourrai t’attendre à l’entrée de l’école.
Amitiés,
Mariam
